# 04/10/2026 11:18 — US–UK–India Economic Cycle Table

Partner, **this is the table I think you were asking me to construct.** I have deliberately not started with AI. I started with the measurable economy and asked: **what powered it → what accumulated → what broke → who got hurt → what government changed → what old structure weakened → what subsequently scaled.**

Official comparable data do **not** start at the same date. UK consistent annual national accounts run back to **1948** and quarterly series to 1955; US modern continuous labour data run from the 1950s while long non-farm industry employment runs to **1939**; India's modern national-account series are generally analysed from **1950/51**, with particularly strong comparable reform-era evidence from 1991 onward. citeturn2search4turn2search10turn2search2

## The comparison

| Period / structural break | 🇺🇸 United States | 🇬🇧 United Kingdom | 🇮🇳 India | **What I think the pattern says** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1950s–60s: post-war economy + first automation fear** | Manufacturing/goods still central; computers and industrial automation appear. Agricultural employment was already collapsing: BLS records 6.45m agricultural workers in 1955 versus a vastly larger non-agricultural economy. citeturn2search2 | Manufacturing remains major; services were only **56% of output even in 1970**. citeturn1search6 | Agriculture dominates employment/output much more strongly; licence/state-directed industrialisation. Computing exists globally but Indian labour cannot yet participate remotely in Western service production. | **Automation exists, but complementary infrastructure is missing.** Technology being technically possible ≠ economically transformative everywhere. |
| **1970s: oil + inflation + industrial stress** | Oil shocks + inflation + unstable stop-go policy. Manufacturing automation/import competition already restructuring labour. | Oil shocks, inflation, union conflict and weak productivity. Industrial model under enormous stress. | Oil-import dependence creates external pressure; regulated/import-substitution economy remains dominant. | An old model becomes progressively harder to sustain **before** the decisive recession/reform. |
| **1979–82 structural break** | Fed deliberately tightens money to kill inflation; fed-funds rate approaches **20%**. Unemployment eventually **10.8%**. Manufacturing/construction hit particularly hard. BLS says automation + import competition amplified manufacturing displacement. citeturn1search1turn1search8 | Oil shock + ~15% inflation + tight fiscal/monetary policy. GDP falls **five consecutive quarters**; unemployment reaches **10.2%**; household spending had a 4.2% quarterly fall. citeturn0search13 | Not equivalent recession yet; 1980s borrowing/fiscal expansion supports faster growth while gradual liberalisation begins. | **US/UK pay the adjustment cost earlier. India postpones its larger regime break.** |
| **What was uprooted?** | High-paying traditional manufacturing, particularly steel and older industrial employment. | Traditional manufacturing/mining model begins much deeper structural decline; later mine closures intensify regional damage. | Licence Raj/state-controlled structure still largely survives. | Recession doesn't *invent* the replacement economy. It **accelerates capital/labour movement away from already weakening structures.** |
| **What grows afterward?** | Services, finance, PCs, software, telecoms and increasingly knowledge work. US nonfarm employment moves progressively from goods to services; goods were **37.6%** of nonfarm jobs in 1939, already only a minority. citeturn2search10 | Services become dominant: **56% of GVA in 1970 → 80% by 2016**. Service employment **15.4m → 28.9m**. citeturn1search6 | 1980s deregulation begins and growth accelerates—but partly through fiscal/external borrowing that proves unsustainable. citeturn0search2turn0search4 | **Employment does not simply disappear. Economic weight migrates.** |
| **1990–91 recession/crisis** | US recession occurs around same global period; information technology and PCs already diffusing. | GDP falls **~2.1–2.2% peak-to-trough**; unemployment **6.9% → 10.6%**; high interest rates, falling house prices and weak investment. citeturn1search3turn1search11 | **Critical regime break.** Fiscal deficits + external borrowing + oil shock + weaker remittances + political uncertainty + capital flight leave reserves near exhaustion. GDP growth collapses to roughly **1–1¾%** in 1991/92 depending on series. Inflation ~13.5%. citeturn0search4turn0search7 | **This is the pivotal row for India.** The crisis destroys the political/economic viability of maintaining the previous model. |
| **Policy response** | Monetary easing/recovery; continued technology investment. | Rates eventually fall; ERM crisis/Black Wednesday follows; economy reorients further toward services/finance. | Devaluation + IMF support + fiscal stabilisation + industrial delicensing + tariff/import liberalisation + FDI liberalisation + financial/tax reforms. Import-weighted tariffs eventually fall **87% (1990/91) → 25% (1996/97)**. citeturn0search3turn0search9 | **Crisis makes politically difficult reforms possible.** This is one of the strongest recurring patterns. |
| **Recovery** | Expansion through 1990s coincides with PC/Internet productivity revolution. | GDP recovers while unemployment peaks later; household balance sheets take longer. | Growth rebounds to about **4½% in 1992/93 and 1993/94, 6¼% by 1994/95**; mid-1990s growth becomes much stronger. citeturn0search3 | GDP recovery occurs **before every damaged worker/community necessarily recovers.** Macro recovery ≠ personal recovery. |
| **1990s → Web/globalisation** | Internet + PCs + enterprise software + capital markets produce extraordinary new-company formation. | Finance/business/professional services expand; manufacturing share keeps shrinking. | Liberalisation + telecom + global corporate IT + English-speaking engineers + wage differential + Y2K/offshoring allow Indian knowledge labour to enter global production. | **1991 didn't create Indian software skill. It removed constraints around skill that already existed.** This matches your point exactly. |
| **2000 dot-com crash** | Technology valuations collapse; many dot-com firms disappear. **Internet infrastructure, software knowledge and users remain.** | Technology/telecom exposure damaged, but no depression. | Global technology downturn affects exports, but offshore-services structure survives and expands later. | **Financial layer dies; useful infrastructure survives.** Failed companies ≠ failed technology. |
| **2001–07 recovery creates next imbalance** | Low rates + securitisation + expanding mortgage credit + housing boom. House prices more than double 1998–2006; mortgage debt **61% → 97% of GDP**; ~40% of net private job creation 2001–05 was housing-related. citeturn1search2 | Credit/property/financial-services boom. | Rapid growth; IT/services/export integration accelerates; global capital integration rises. | **The solution/recovery regime itself eventually produces new excesses.** This is another part of your cycle. |
| **2008–09 Great Recession** | Housing/credit structure breaks. GDP **−4.3% peak-to-trough**; unemployment <5% → **10%**; houses ~−30%; S&P −57%; household net worth ~$69tn → ~$55tn. citeturn1search4 | GDP **−6.1%**, five-quarter contraction; deepest modern downturn then. Pre-crisis GDP level not regained until **Q2 2013**. citeturn1search12 | Growth slows sharply but India avoids the banking-system collapse seen in US/UK; earlier reforms and more limited toxic-asset exposure provide some insulation. | **Same global shock, different damage because economic structures differ.** |
| **Government response** | Rates → ~0; bank/liquidity rescue; fiscal stimulus; QE1 eventually ~**$1.75tn** long-term asset purchases. citeturn1search4 | Bank rescues, rate cuts, fiscal support, later QE and subsequent fiscal consolidation. | Monetary/fiscal support; liquidity; government expenditure/investment measures. | When private circulation breaks, **the state becomes balance-sheet/demand stabiliser.** Exactly the economic loop you raised. |
| **Who gets uprooted?** | Construction, mortgage finance, banking; millions lose jobs/homes/wealth. | Finance, construction and related industries; real wages/living standards suffer; recovery unusually weak. | Export/manufacturing sectors affected but structural domestic transformation continues. | Crisis reallocates not just workers but **capital, political legitimacy and risk tolerance.** |
| **What scales after 2008?** | Cloud, smartphones, SaaS, social networks, streaming, fintech, gig economy. | Digital services, fintech, e-commerce, platform economy. | Mobile/Internet economy, IT services, digital payments, startups and global engineering/services. | **Most were incubating before the crash. The crash didn't invent them. It changed the environment in which they scaled.** |
| **2020 COVID shock** | Artificial shutdown; extraordinary fiscal/monetary transfers preserve income/demand; digital adoption jumps. | Historically huge output collapse; government wage support preserves household/employment connection. | Lockdowns devastate informal/contact-intensive work; digitisation accelerates sharply. | A near laboratory demonstration: governments deliberately prevented **lost production → lost income → lost demand → further lost production** from fully cascading. |
| **2022–26 AI transition** | Services/knowledge economy now dominant; AI attacks tasks inside the sector that absorbed labour from earlier mechanisation. | ~service-dominated economy; same exposure. | Huge service/IT workforce created partly by the previous globalisation/digital wave is now directly exposed to AI productivity. | **This is unusual:** AI is attacking the *destination* into which labour moved during previous waves. That deserves serious attention. |

---

## The pattern I now see

Your hypothesis needs one modification.

It isn't:

> recession → new technology.

It is much closer to:

> **technology + credit + policy + demographics + existing institutions create a growth regime → that regime develops imbalances → shock exposes the weakest assumptions → recession destroys/weakens parts of the old allocation → government changes monetary/fiscal/regulatory rules → capital searches for higher-return uses → technologies already incubating become economically viable → new industries absorb capital/labour → expansion → new imbalance.**

Or compactly:

**INCUBATION → BOOM → IMBALANCE → SHOCK → RECESSION → CLEARING/INTERVENTION → REALLOCATION → NEW SCALE → BOOM**

genui{"learning_viz":{"type_id":"BUSINESS_CYCLES"}}

The normal business-cycle picture above is useful, but **our model adds structural technological change underneath it**.

---

## Now look at the three countries differently

This is where I think it becomes powerful.

### 🇺🇸 US — **technology/capital generator**

The US repeatedly generates or massively finances the next technical infrastructure:

**mass production → computers → semiconductor → PC → Internet → cloud → mobile/platforms → AI.**

When a crash occurs, enormous capital destruction happens—but technical capability often remains.

2008 is especially revealing. The US lost 4.3% of real GDP peak-to-trough, unemployment doubled to 10%, household net worth lost roughly $14 trillion, and housing collapsed. citeturn1search4

Yet AWS, smartphones, cloud software, social networks and digital platforms did not disappear.

They became part of the **next economic structure**.

---

### 🇬🇧 UK — **structural reallocator**

The UK gives us perhaps the cleanest long-term example of employment/output moving rather than simply disappearing.

In 1970:

**services = 56% of the economy.**

By 2016:

**services = 80%.**

And service employment:

**15.4 million → 28.9 million.** citeturn1search6

Yet during that same period Britain experienced devastating losses in:

- mining,
- manufacturing,
- traditional industrial communities.

So both statements are simultaneously true:

> **Technology/economic restructuring destroyed livelihoods.**

AND

> **The total economy found enormous amounts of other work.**

This distinction is absolutely central to the AI debate.

---

### 🇮🇳 India — **late integration / constraint removal**

India is even more interesting.

The human capability did **not suddenly appear in 1991**.

Engineers existed.

Universities existed.

Mathematics existed.

Industrial capability existed.

Computing expertise existed.

What changed was the **economic system around those capabilities**.

Before 1991:

```text id="dh7jnc"
capability
+
licensing
+
high tariffs
+
capital restrictions
+
weak telecom
+
limited global integration

= constrained economic output
```

After reforms + telecommunications + global digitalisation:

```text id="nlpqy3"
capability
+
global markets
+
telecommunications
+
capital
+
software demand
+
wage differential

= exportable knowledge labour
```

The crisis became the political forcing mechanism.

And the numbers after reform are striking: India moved from the crisis-era growth collapse to roughly 4½% growth in 1992/93–93/94 and 6¼% by 1994/95; mid-1990s growth became substantially stronger. citeturn0search3turn0search6

That is not:

> “WWW created India.”

It is:

> **multiple previously disconnected ingredients became economically connected.**

---

# The most important row is actually 2008

Because look at what happens around the following decade.

The financial economy is devastated.

But simultaneously:

```text id="vdfywo"
iPhone       2007
Android      2008
AWS          scaling
cloud        scaling
Facebook     scaling
YouTube      scaling
streaming    scaling
smartphones  scaling
mobile apps  scaling
```

These technologies weren't created *by* the recession.

They were **already gestating.**

Then you have:

```text id="vlr4zx"
recession
     ↓
old businesses weakened
capital repriced
labour available
consumer behaviour changing
infrastructure already ready
     ↓
NEW MODEL CAN SCALE
```

This is much closer to your **“chaos is opportunity”** statement.

---

# And now I think I see what you're trying to get me to infer about AI

We should **not start with ChatGPT in 2022.**

That is too late.

For the current cycle, incubation probably looks something like:

```text id="0c1p99"
2008–12
cloud + smartphone + huge digital-data creation
          ↓
2012–17
deep learning + GPUs
          ↓
2017
transformer
          ↓
2018–21
foundation-model scaling
          ↓
2020
COVID → forced global digitisation
          ↓
2022
ChatGPT → mass interface
          ↓
2023–25
multimodal + coding + RAG + tools
          ↓
2025–26
agents + computer use + cheap software production
          ↓
???
STRUCTURAL ECONOMIC EVENT
          ↓
???
NEXT EQUILIBRIUM
```

And **that `???` is more important than predicting whether today's coding job loses 30% or 60% of its tasks.**

---

# One thing is materially different this time

Look at where labour moved historically.

```text id="3f97nc"
AGRICULTURE
     ↓
MANUFACTURING
     ↓
SERVICES
     ↓
KNOWLEDGE WORK
```

Mechanisation attacked agriculture.

Industrial automation attacked manufacturing.

Internet/software expanded knowledge work.

But now:

# AI attacks knowledge work itself.

That's important.

Where does displaced labour move **next**?

We cannot simply say:

> “services.”

They're already there.

We cannot simply say:

> “software.”

AI directly increases software productivity.

So the historical model tells us there **should be a new scarcity/demand frontier**, but it does **not tell us automatically what it is**.

That is precisely the forecasting problem worth solving.

---

# And your purchasing-power argument constrains the answer

Whatever comes next cannot sustainably be:

```text id="gncj0w"
AI owns production
↓
companies employ nobody
↓
people earn nothing
↓
people consume nothing
↓
companies somehow become enormously valuable
```

That loop breaks.

Therefore one or several variables must adjust:

```text id="2bvz9e"
NEW jobs
or
NEW human activities
or
working hours ↓
or
prices ↓ dramatically
or
capital ownership broadens
or
government redistribution ↑
or
AI-generated surplus distributed differently
or
some combination
```

That's not ideology.

That's an accounting/economic constraint.

---

# My first actual forecast from this table

I wouldn't forecast **“90% unemployment.”**

I would forecast something more subtle:

> **AI first causes a large fall in labour-hours required per unit of cognitive output, rather than an equivalent fall in total employment.**

That creates:

**productivity shock → price compression → enormous increase in quantity/variety of cognitive products → destruction of some existing firms/jobs → explosion of previously uneconomic services → new bottlenecks/scarcities → labour/capital migration.**

Exactly as:

```text id="w3oq5i"
less labour / shirt
≠
no clothing workers

less labour / computation
≠
no computer workers

less labour / webpage
≠
no Internet workers

less labour / software unit
≠ necessarily
no software economy
```

It may instead produce **vastly more software**.

And that's where our earlier discussion about reusable AI infrastructure becomes more interesting.

---

## The question I think you were trying to make me discover

Not:

> **“Which jobs will AI destroy?”**

Not:

> **“Is AI another Internet?”**

Not even:

> **“What will the next recession be?”**

It is:

# **When intelligence becomes dramatically cheaper, what new economic activity becomes possible at such scale that it absorbs the money, capital and human activity released from today's expensive cognitive work?**

That is the unknown variable.

And now we have a way to attack it quantitatively rather than asking me to make a clever prediction: take US/UK/India from the earliest reliable series, construct **sector GDP + sector employment + productivity + wages/income + consumption + taxation + technology adoption + recession + policy intervention** through time, and measure *where economic value migrated after every productivity shock*.

That would turn the table above into something much more useful: a **historical transition model**, from which we can test candidate AI futures instead of simply guessing them.

# 14/10/2026 14:52 — Stop Expanding, Build the System

Partner, I understand why you're tired. **You should not have had to keep discovering one missing variable at a time for me**—employment, then hidden unemployment, then government financing, then investment, then cost of capital, then expectations.

The problem is now clear: we've been **adding variables reactively instead of designing the complete system first**.

So I am changing the approach. **No more adding another clever variable after every discussion.** Before building anything, the research model needs a completeness audit across the whole economic system.

The object we are really trying to construct is not an “AI jobs model.” It is a **technology–economy–human transition model** that happens to be used to investigate AI.

## The complete model boundary

I would freeze these **12 interacting systems** before implementation:

| # | System | What must be represented | What we were missing |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Population** | population, age, migration, households, working-age population | Demography changes both labour supply and demand |
| 2 | **Labour** | employment, unemployment, participation, hours, occupations, skills | We originally overfocused on unemployment |
| 3 | **Hidden labour stress** | inactivity, discouraged workers, involuntary part-time, informal/farm absorption, self-employment, pay squeeze | Your correction |
| 4 | **Households** | wages, capital income, transfers, tax, debt, savings, consumption, housing | Determines whether productivity becomes demand |
| 5 | **Industry** | sector GDP, employment, wages, productivity, prices, profits, closures/formation | Shows exactly where transition occurs |
| 6 | **Business capital** | investment, depreciation, capacity, R&D, inventories, cash, leverage | Determines future productive capacity |
| 7 | **Finance** | credit, banks, equity, VC, bond yields, asset prices, defaults | Determines where capital can flow |
| 8 | **Capital expectations** | expected ROI, cost of capital, risk premium, uncertainty, valuation | Your latest major correction |
| 9 | **Government** | taxes, spending, benefits, investment, deficit, debt, interest | Government cannot give resources for free |
| 10 | **Central bank / money** | rates, money/credit, liquidity, QE/QT, inflation, currency | Determines financing conditions and crisis propagation |
| 11 | **External economy** | trade, FX, capital flows, reserves, outsourcing/offshoring, commodity prices | Essential for India and global shocks |
| 12 | **Technology & institutions** | capability, adoption, cost, regulation, infrastructure, business model, work method | Separates invention from economic adoption |

But there are **four cross-cutting forces** that cannot simply be another row.

### A. Distribution

Who receives the productivity surplus?

**labour / owners / investors / government / consumers through lower prices / foreign economy**

Two economies can have identical GDP growth and completely different human outcomes.

### B. Expectations and behaviour

Workers, consumers, investors, firms and governments react to what they **think will happen**, not merely what has already happened.

Fear can therefore create a feedback loop:

**job fear → saving ↑ → spending ↓ → revenue ↓ → hiring ↓ → fear confirmed.**

Optimism can do the opposite—and can also create bubbles.

### C. Geography and inequality

National averages hide:

**region + age + education + occupation + income + gender + urban/rural differences.**

A country can recover while a former industrial town does not.

### D. Time

We need several clocks simultaneously:

**invention → specialist use → investment boom → mass adoption → productivity → labour displacement → retraining → new demand → institutional adaptation.**

These lags are absolutely essential.

---

## One major thing we still hadn't modelled properly: **business births and deaths**

Workers don't merely migrate between existing industries.

New firms appear.

Old firms disappear.

So:

**technology → old-company productivity pressure → failures/consolidation + startups/new business models → different employment structure.**

That is how we capture something like:

mainframe → PC firms → Internet firms → cloud firms → mobile firms → AI firms.

Without firm creation/destruction, our simulation would force tomorrow's workers into today's industries.

That would make forecasting structurally wrong.

---

## Another missing piece: **prices and demand elasticity**

Suppose AI makes software production **80% cheaper**.

That tells us almost nothing about employment until we know:

> If software becomes 80% cheaper, how much more software will humanity consume?

If demand increases 2×, employment may fall.

If demand increases 20×, employment could increase despite enormous productivity growth.

Historically this mechanism matters enormously.

Therefore every sector needs:

\[
DemandResponse_i=f(Price_i,\ Income,\ NewUses,\ Substitutes)
\]

This may be **more important than technical automation percentage**.

---

## Another: **complementarity versus substitution**

AI doesn't just substitute humans.

Some capital makes humans more productive.

Therefore each occupation/task needs two coefficients:

**substitution exposure** and **complementarity exposure**.

A radiologist, programmer, teacher, accountant and cleaner can all have high AI relevance while having completely different employment effects.

---

## Another: **physical bottlenecks**

Cognition becoming cheap doesn't make:

- land,
- housing,
- electricity,
- chips,
- construction,
- minerals,
- logistics,
- healthcare capacity,
- physical care,
- grid connections

automatically abundant.

So AI can move scarcity from **cognition → physical resources**.

That could create employment and investment somewhere completely different.

---

## Another: **ownership**

This is enormous and we hadn't given it enough importance.

If households indirectly own AI capital through:

- pensions,
- shares,
- mutual funds,
- sovereign funds,

then automation profits can return to households **without wages**.

If ownership is extremely concentrated, they don't circulate the same way.

Therefore:

\[
HouseholdIncome =
LabourIncome+
CapitalIncome+
Transfers
\]

The future cannot be modelled from wages alone.

---

## Another: **international comparative advantage**

AI could simultaneously:

**reduce India's labour-cost advantage**

and

**multiply each Indian worker's productive capacity.**

Likewise it could make a tiny UK firm export globally or allow US companies to reshore cognitive work.

Therefore AI can alter:

\[
ComparativeAdvantage(country,sector)
\]

That changes trade, FX, wages and employment.

---

# The master historical panel

Now I would freeze the research object as:

### 🇺🇸 US: 1929–2026

```text
wage differential
        +
Y2K/global outsourcing
        ↓
INDIAN IT EXPORT ECONOMY
```

And we have a quantitative marker:

| Year | Indian services exports | Software share |
|---|---:|---:|
| 1970–71 | $0.3bn | **0%** |
| 1980–81 | $2.8bn | **0%** |
| 1990–91 | $4.6bn | **0%** |
| 2000–01 | $16.3bn | **39.0%** |
| 2005–06 | $57.7bn | **40.9%** |
| 2008–09 | software exports alone **$47bn** | — |

RBI official historical data. citeturn2search5

**This is exactly the type of structural emergence our AI simulation needs to allow.**

If our model merely destroys jobs without allowing an entirely new sector to appear, it is historically biased.

---

# 7. The most important verified economic-loop evidence

The historical evidence supports your original purchasing-power argument surprisingly well.

### UK 2008

GDP falls.

Employment falls.

But household income **initially doesn't fall proportionately**.

Why?

ONS explicitly explains that:

- mortgage payments fell because rates fell;
- people paid less tax;
- social-security benefits increased.

Consequently real household income per head was actually **3.8% above its pre-recession level by Q2 2009**. citeturn6search4

That's our loop:

```text
MARKET INCOME ↓
      ↓
tax paid ↓
benefits ↑
interest burden ↓
      ↓
DISPOSABLE INCOME partially protected
      ↓
CONSUMPTION protected
      ↓
GDP decline limited
```

This is exactly one of the mechanisms we need in the simulator.

---

# 8. COVID gives us an even cleaner experiment

### US

Government pandemic legislation:

**+$2.3tn FY2020 deficit**

and CBO estimated:

**GDP level +4.7% in 2020 compared with absence of that legislation.** citeturn0search7

### UK

Instead of allowing employer → worker income connection to break:

**8.9 million jobs/employments were furloughed at peak.** citeturn1search12

### India

Instead of allowing financial conditions to tighten during collapsing activity:

**repo → 4%**, with large targeted liquidity/credit support. citeturn3search5

Three different institutional systems.

Same underlying objective:

# Prevent the economic circulation from collapsing.

---

# 9. The historical pattern table

This is now the table I would actually use as the intellectual basis of our model.

| Stage | 1930s | 1980s | 1990s | 2008 | 2020 | AI scenario |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Existing engine | industry | manufacturing | services/early IT | finance/property/globalisation | service/digital economy | knowledge/services |
| Accumulated vulnerability | credit/banking | inflation/industrial weakness | property/debt or India external imbalance | leverage/housing | pandemic vulnerability | **? labour-income dependence** |
| Trigger | banking/market | monetary tightening/oil | credit/external crisis | financial system | health shutdown | **AI productivity shock?** |
| Labour hit | huge | manufacturing | construction/finance etc. | finance/construction | contact services | cognitive/service tasks |
| Income ↓ | extreme | significant | significant | significant | potentially enormous | **model variable** |
| Consumption ↓ | extreme | yes | yes | yes | administratively interrupted | **model variable** |
| Tax receipts ↓ | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes | **model variable** |
| Government support ↑ | eventually | stabilisation | monetary/reform | very large | enormous | **model variable** |
| Rates ↓ after shock | yes/eventually | after inflation defeated | yes | near zero | near zero | **model variable** |
| Old structure damaged | banking/old industry | manufacturing | old regulation/intermediation | leveraged finance | physical/contact model | **human-cost cognitive production?** |
| Existing new technology scales | mass production/electrification | PC/electronics | Internet/software | cloud/mobile | digital/remote/AI | **agents/robotics/?** |
| New demand created | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes | **must be endogenous** |
| New scarcity | industrial capacity | skills/services | distribution/data | mobile/cloud ecosystems | digital capacity | **trust? physical execution? demand? ownership? human attention?** |

---

# 10. What the simulation therefore must contain

A simple model containing only:

```text
AI ↑
→ productivity ↑
→ workers ↓
```

will produce nonsense.

We need at minimum:

\[
GDP = C + I + G + NX
\]

and household consumption needs something like:

\[
C_t=f(W_t + B_t + K_t - T_t,\; confidence,\; prices)
\]

where:

- **W** = wages/labour income
- **B** = government transfers
- **K** = capital/dividend income
- **T** = tax.

Businesses:

\[
Profit_t = Revenue_t-Wages_t-AIcost_t-OtherCosts_t
\]

Government:

\[
Balance_t = Taxes_t - Transfers_t-G_t
\]

AI productivity:

\[
Output/Worker \uparrow
\]

but then crucially:

\[
Price \downarrow
\rightarrow Demand \uparrow
\rightarrow Output \uparrow
\rightarrow Employment\ response
\]

And we need another term that most AI-job forecasts omit:

# New demand.

Something like:

\[
NewSector_t =
f(CostReduction,\ Technology,\ Capital,\ HumanNeeds,\ Time)
\]

Without that variable, the model would have predicted catastrophic permanent unemployment from mechanisation, computers and the Internet.

---

# 11. One more variable is essential: distribution of AI surplus

Suppose AI creates **£100 of additional productivity**.

Scenario 1:

```text
£70 → wages
£20 → profits
£10 → tax
```

Very different economy from:

```text
£5 → wages
£90 → profits
£5 → tax
```

Even though:

# GDP productivity is identical.

Why?

Because the **marginal propensity to consume** differs.

That feeds directly into:

```text
income distribution
      ↓
consumption
      ↓
company revenue
      ↓
investment
      ↓
employment
      ↓
tax
      ↺
```

So our simulator needs a parameter such as:

### `labour_share_of_AI_surplus`

and another:

### `capital_share_of_AI_surplus`

This may prove much more important than the headline:

### `% tasks automated`.

---

# 12. The historical recovery benchmark we can calibrate against

| Country / shock | GDP damage | Labour damage | Major intervention | GDP recovery character |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| US Great Depression | enormous/multi-year | ~12.8m unemployed under broad 1933 estimate | banking/New Deal/monetary institutional changes | **years; interrupted again 1937** citeturn0search2turn0search10 |
| US 1981–82 | severe | unemployment annual **9.7%**, peak nearly 11% | inflation eventually broken/rates fall | comparatively fast once monetary constraint released citeturn0search4turn5search4 |
| UK 1973–75 | **−5.4%** | unemployment rising | macro adjustment | **14 quarters** citeturn6search1 |
| UK 1980–81 | **−4.5%** | manufacturing devastated | macro/structural adjustment | **13 quarters** citeturn6search1turn1search7 |
| UK 1990–92 | **−2.9%** | unemployment peak **10.6% quarterly** | monetary/exchange-rate adjustment | **14 quarters** citeturn6search1turn6search2 |
| UK 2008–09 | **−6.3%** | unemployment rises materially | bank rescue + low rates + **£200bn QE** | **21 quarters** citeturn6search9turn1search9 |
| US 2008–09 | approx **−4.3%** Fed historical estimate | unemployment peak **10%** | zero rates + financial intervention + **~$1.75tn QE1** | GDP recession ends 2009; labour recovery much slower citeturn0search5 |
| India 2008–09 | growth slows to **6.7%**, not contraction | sector/export stress | fiscal stimulus ~**3% GDP**, repo −425bp | relatively fast rebound citeturn2search3turn2search4 |
| US COVID | annual **−2.1% current vintage** | Q2 unemployment **13%** | enormous household/business support | very fast GDP rebound citeturn5search0turn0search3 |
| UK COVID | annual **−10.0% current series** | furlough peak **8.9m** | wage replacement/furlough + monetary/fiscal support | unusually fast initial rebound citeturn8search1turn1search12 |
| India COVID | **−6.6% FY20/21** | severe informal/contact-sector disruption | fiscal/credit/liquidity + repo 4% | ~**9.2% initial FY21/22 estimate** citeturn3search2turn3search0 |

---

## The most important conclusion before simulation

The verified historical data **do not support** a simple law:

> recession → technology → recovery.

They support something more useful:

> **A shock destroys income and demand. The depth of the recession depends partly on how strongly that income-demand feedback is allowed to run. Policy interrupts that loop. Meanwhile, recessions accelerate reallocation away from already-vulnerable sectors. Technologies and business models that were incubating before the crisis can then capture disproportionate investment, labour and demand during the subsequent expansion.**

And now we have something we did **not** have at the beginning of today's discussion:

### a falsifiable AI hypothesis.

If AI removes labour income faster than **(a)** prices fall, **(b)** new demand forms, **(c)** new sectors absorb labour, **(d)** capital income reaches households, or **(e)** government recycles the surplus, then:

**wages ↓ → consumption ↓ → revenue ↓ → investment ↓ → employment ↓ → tax ↓ → recessionary feedback.**

If productivity gains circulate sufficiently through those five channels, we instead get:

**productivity ↑ → prices ↓ / real income ↑ → consumption/new demand ↑ → investment ↑ → new economic activity ↑ → employment restructures rather than disappears.**

That is the **historical fork** our US–UK–India AI simulation should test. The important input will not merely be “AI automates X%.” It will be **how fast automation happens versus how fast purchasing power and new demand are regenerated.**

parts:
# 04/10/2026 14:07 — Deep Model + History Replay

Partner, **yes: the previous tables are still only the top of the iceberg.** I searched deeper after your correction, including current official sources and contemporary official records. I would **not yet run an AI forecast** from the previous model.

The model needs two layers:

1. **Economic anatomy** — reconstruct what the whole country actually looked like around every major transition.
2. **Replay validation** — hide the outcome, inject the historical shock, and see whether our equations reproduce what subsequently happened.

Only after passing layer 2 should we allow it to say anything meaningful about AI.

One correction first: unemployment has absolutely exceeded 5–10%. In the US Depression, retrospective BLS estimates put unemployment at **12.83 million in 1933** under the broad relief-worker definition, versus 1.55 million in 1929. citeturn0search2 So we need population, labour force and employment counts—not just percentages.

---

## 1. The dataset should look like this

Instead of my previous 10-column recession table, **each country × year/quarter** needs something closer to this:

| Layer | Variables we need |
|---|---|
| Population | population, working-age population, labour force |
| Labour | employed, unemployed, participation, hours worked |
| Employment anatomy | agriculture, manufacturing, construction, mining, retail, finance, professional, government, health, education, etc. |
| Production | real/nominal GDP, GDP per capita, productivity |
| GDP anatomy | value added by every major industry |
| Income | wages, profits, mixed/self-employed income, transfers |
| Household | disposable income, consumption, savings, debt |
| Prices | CPI/inflation, asset prices, housing |
| Business | investment, inventories, profits, failures |
| Government | tax receipts by type, spending, transfers, deficit |
| Government financing | borrowing, debt stock, interest cost |
| Central bank | rates, money/credit, QE/QT/balance sheet |
| External | exports, imports, current account, FX, reserves |
| Technology | prevailing production method and adoption |
| Work method | what humans actually did and how it changed |
| Shock | oil/war/rates/credit/pandemic/technology/etc. |
| Remedy | rates/tax/spending/transfers/regulation/restructuring |
| Transition | occupations/industries declining and expanding |
| Recovery | GDP recovery, employment recovery, income recovery |
| Distribution | who actually captured the subsequent productivity gain |

**That is the economic organism.**

GDP alone is only its temperature.

---

# 2. Your 1929 correction is important

The Depression cannot be reduced to:

> stock market crashed → recession.

The official Federal Reserve history itself gives a much richer sequence.

During the 1920s, automobiles, telephones and other new technologies were spreading rapidly. Brokerage houses, investment trusts and margin accounts expanded access to equities. Investors commonly put down only around **10%** and borrowed the remainder. citeturn0search1

Meanwhile, the Fed had loosened conditions in 1924 and 1927 partly to support recovery and the post-WWI international monetary system. By 1928 it became worried about financial speculation and tightened. citeturn0search4turn0search5

Then:

**WWI aftermath / gold-standard problems → credit conditions → 1920s productivity & technology boom → equity speculation/leverage → monetary tightening → 1929 contraction/crash → consumption/investment decline → banking panics → money supply collapse → deflation → real debt burden ↑ → bankruptcies → unemployment → demand ↓↓**

The banking panics are critical. The Fed's history says the economy appeared capable of recovering from the initial crash before banking crises beginning in late 1930 transformed the downturn into the Great Depression. citeturn0search7

And from fall 1930 to winter 1933:

**money supply fell nearly 30%.** citeturn0search0

So this is already teaching our simulation something:

> **A shock alone doesn't determine the outcome. Feedback loops and policy response determine amplification.**

---

# 3. And look at unemployment through the Depression

This is far more informative than one peak number.

| Year | US unemployed — relief workers treated unemployed |
|---:|---:|
| 1929 | **1.55m** |
| 1930 | **4.34m** |
| 1931 | **8.02m** |
| 1932 | **12.06m** |
| 1933 | **12.83m** |
| 1934 | **11.34m** |
| 1935 | **10.61m** |
| 1936 | **9.03m** |
| 1937 | **7.70m** |
| 1938 | **10.39m** |
| 1939 | **9.48m** |
| 1940 | **8.12m** |
| 1941 | **5.56m** |
| 1942 | **2.66m** |
| 1943 | **1.07m** |

These are retrospective historical estimates documented by BLS; importantly, BLS explains that 1930s labour statistics were not collected using today's system, so the uncertainty must remain in our model. citeturn0search2

Now something becomes obvious.

This was **not**:

> crash → 10% unemployment → government gives money → normal.

It took **years**, another recession occurred in 1937, and wartime mobilisation finally coincides with the enormous final employment absorption.

That's a fundamentally different transition from 2020.

---

# 4. Now compare that with 2008 sector-by-sector

This is where my earlier table was far too shallow.

US BLS finds that nearly **two-thirds of recession job losses** were concentrated in just three sectors:

**construction + manufacturing + administrative/support services.**

Construction alone lost more than **1.5 million jobs**, almost **21%** of its employment, December 2007–October 2009. citeturn1search6

BEA tells us what was happening on the production side.

Already in **2007**, before the recognised recession had fully unfolded:

- construction value added: **−11.2%**
- finance/insurance growth: slowed to **0.1% from 6.3%**
- durable manufacturing: slowed materially. citeturn1search3

Then in 2008:

- manufacturing value added: **−2.7%**
- retail: **−0.5%**
- finance/insurance: **−3.0%**. citeturn1search0

And manufacturing deterioration intensified subsequently. citeturn1search7turn1search17

### That's much more useful.

The recession didn't suddenly appear in September 2008.

The model was deteriorating **before the dramatic event**.

---

# 5. That gives us another variable

Call it:

## **Structural Stress Index — SSI**

For every sector:

\[
SSI_i =
f(
productivity,
employment,
wages,
profits,
investment,
debt,
prices,
imports,
technology,
demand
)
\]

Imagine construction in 2006:

```text
employment ↑
house prices ↑↑
mortgage credit ↑↑
debt ↑↑
construction ↑
```

It superficially looks healthy.

But:

```text
income supporting debt
<
asset-price/credit expansion
```

Then vulnerability is accumulating.

That's why **GDP growth alone cannot identify the problem.**

---

# 6. Now 2020 gives the opposite experiment

COVID hit different sectors entirely.

In Q1 2020 US BEA measured:

| Industry | Real value-added movement |
|---|---:|
| Accommodation/food | **−26.8%** |
| Arts/entertainment/recreation | **−34.7%** |
| Finance/insurance | **−9.0%** |
| Health/social assistance | **−7.8%** |
| Agriculture | **+15.5%** |

citeturn1search2

And Q2 became vastly more severe. Accommodation/food and healthcare were among the largest contributors to the collapse. citeturn1search10turn1search12

But look at something fascinating in the annual data.

While most activity contracted:

> **information increased**, particularly data processing and Internet-related activity.

Software investment also increased while many other forms of non-residential investment declined. citeturn1search1

There it is.

### Crisis destroys one mode while accelerating another already-existing mode.

Not because COVID invented Internet/cloud/software.

Because those technologies were already mature enough to absorb activity.

---

# 7. This is exactly what we need to measure around every recession

For each major episode:

### Five years BEFORE

What technology/work practice was already spreading?

### At the PEAK

Which industries looked strongest?

### Two years before

Which underlying variables had already started weakening?

### Shock

What actually broke?

### Trough

Which workers/industries absorbed the damage?

### Intervention

Where did the money come from and where did it go?

### 1–5 years AFTER

Where did workers go?

### 5–10 years AFTER

Which technology/business structure became normal?

That's much closer to the research you're asking for.

---

# 8. Government spending — your correction is exactly right

I used language like:

> “government injects money.”

That's insufficient.

There is **no free government resource**.

The complete circuit is:

```text
TAX
   \
BORROWING → GOVERNMENT → SPENDING/TRANSFERS
   /                         ↓
MONEY/CB                   ECONOMY
                             ↓
                         future tax base
```

If borrowing finances support:

\[
Debt_{t+1}=Debt_t+Deficit_t
\]

Then:

\[
InterestCost_{t+1}
\approx Debt_{t+1}\times InterestRate
\]

So today's stabilisation can become tomorrow's:

- interest expense,
- taxation requirement,
- reduced fiscal space,
- inflation risk,
- currency pressure,
- crowding-out risk.

Depending on conditions.

---

# 9. And central-bank financing isn't free either

Suppose central bank purchases government bonds.

That can:

- lower yields,
- increase liquidity,
- raise asset prices,
- alter credit conditions,
- affect currency,
- eventually interact with inflation.

And unwinding has consequences too.

Interestingly, current Bank of England research finds QE effects are **state-dependent**: later rounds do not necessarily behave like earlier rounds. citeturn0search8

That means our model **cannot use one fixed “£1 QE = X GDP” multiplier forever.**

That's extremely important for AI simulation.

---

# 10. The government module therefore needs a balance sheet

Not merely:

```text
government_spending = X
```

But:

| Government variable | Model |
|---|---|
| tax revenue | income + consumption + corporate + property etc. |
| expenditure | services + investment + transfers |
| deficit | expenditure − receipts |
| borrowing | new debt issued |
| debt | accumulated deficits/adjustments |
| interest | debt × effective rate |
| central-bank holdings | monetary-policy interaction |
| inflation | purchasing-power consequence |
| future tax | possible adjustment channel |
| real services | resource use, not merely money |
| transfers | redistribution, not direct production |

This distinction matters:

### Government builds a railway

Resources are used to create productive capital.

### Government sends £1,000 transfer

Purchasing power moves between balance sheets.

Both increase spending somewhere.

They are **not economically identical**.

---

# 11. Now India 2008 — your observation is basically the right direction

India did **not experience a US/UK-style domestic financial collapse**.

Its GDP still grew around **6.7% in FY2008–09** rather than contracting.

So our replay must not feed:

```text
GLOBAL CRISIS = -X GDP
```

to every country.

Instead:

\[
CountryImpact =
GlobalShock
\times Exposure
\times DomesticVulnerability
\times PolicyResponse
\]

That explains why:

```text
same 2008 world
      ↓
US → deep recession
UK → deep recession
India → sharp slowdown, but positive growth
```

This is exactly the kind of thing the simulation must reproduce.

---

# 12. And offshoring must be explicitly modelled

You're also right that we cannot write:

> US job moved to India = US unemployment rises permanently by one.

Suppose:

```text
100 US IT jobs
       ↓
40 automated/offshored
```

Possible outcome:

```text
40 old jobs disappear

BUT

company cost ↓
price ↓
profit ↑
investment ↑

US:
cloud jobs ↑
architecture ↑
product jobs ↑
sales ↑
management ↑
new companies ↑

India:
development ↑
support ↑
BPO ↑
income ↑
consumption ↑

GLOBAL:
software price ↓
software usage ↑↑
```

Therefore we need a **worker-transition matrix**.

---

# 13. Worker Transition Matrix

For every displaced worker cohort:

\[
P_{ij} =
P(worker\ moves\ from\ sector\ i\rightarrow j)
\]

Example:

| From ↓ / To → | Same sector/new role | New sector | Unemployed | Leaves labour force | Self-employed |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Manufacturing | x | x | x | x | x |
| Construction | x | x | x | x | x |
| IT | x | x | x | x | x |
| Clerical | x | x | x | x | x |

And transitions depend on:

- age,
- education,
- geography,
- wage,
- retraining time,
- new-industry growth,
- unemployment duration.

**This is the missing bridge between “jobs destroyed” and national unemployment.**

---

# 14. Technology also needs its own timeline

Your point about Ab Initio/GDE/no-code is exactly why.

We need three dates:

| Technology | Invention | Specialist adoption | Mass/economic adoption |
|---|---|---|---|
| computer | early | specialist | later |
| mainframe | — | enterprises | — |
| PC | — | early users | 1980s/90s |
| visual development | — | specialist | later |
| Internet | research network | technical users | 1990s |
| cloud | technical precursor | early web firms | late 2000s/2010s |
| deep learning | decades of precursors | research | 2010s |
| LLM | research evolution | AI community | 2020s |
| ChatGPT | — | — | **2022 mass interface** |
| coding agents | precursor tools | developers | **2024–26 acceleration** |

Therefore:

> **technology age ≠ mass-economic-impact age.**

That's exactly why “AI started in 2022” is nonsense for our economic model.

2022 is an **access/adoption discontinuity**, not AI's birth.

---

# 15. Your programming argument also changes the model

We should model software development as an abstraction ladder:

```text
machine instruction
     ↓
assembly
     ↓
higher-level language
     ↓
libraries
     ↓
framework
     ↓
visual/GDE
     ↓
declarative/no-code
     ↓
AI code generation
     ↓
agentic development
```

Each step does approximately:

\[
HumanInstructionsPerOutput \downarrow
\]

while:

\[
SoftwareOutputPerWorker \uparrow
\]

That is the variable we should compare historically.

Not:

> “Is AI coding unprecedented?”

But:

> **How large is this abstraction/productivity jump compared with previous abstraction jumps?**

That is measurable in principle.

---

# 16. Your own 23-year observation matters conceptually

Writing code contains cognition.

But it also contains enormous amounts of:

- syntax,
- boilerplate,
- repetition,
- search,
- integration,
- translation of known patterns,
- debugging mundane problems.

AI attacks these first.

Therefore:

```text
developer work
=
problem understanding
+ architecture
+ domain reasoning
+ implementation
+ verification
+ maintenance
```

AI doesn't need to eliminate that equation.

It can massively shrink:

### `implementation`.

Then human work moves toward the remaining terms.

Which is precisely what abstraction layers have repeatedly done.

The magnitude may be new.

The mechanism isn't.

---

# 17. Now your AI-panic question — there really was an observable 2026 escalation

Your memory about February 2026 is correct.

On **4 February 2026**, Reuters reported that nearly **$1 trillion** had been wiped from global software/services stocks amid fear that AI tools could directly attack valuable software businesses. The S&P software/services index had fallen for six consecutive sessions, around **13%**, and about **26% from its October peak**. citeturn0news138

That's a valuable marker.

We should add another series:

## **AI Economic Fear Index**

Starting around ChatGPT's mass release:

```text
2022
2023
2024
2025
2026
```

Measure annually/monthly:

- Google search interest: AI + jobs/unemployment
- news-article volume
- earnings-call mentions
- layoff announcements citing AI
- surveys asking workers about AI job loss
- stock-market events attributed to AI substitution
- job-posting changes by exposed occupation
- wages in exposed occupations
- graduate employment in exposed fields.

Then distinguish:

```text
FEAR INDEX
versus
REAL LABOUR DISPLACEMENT INDEX
```

That could be fascinating.

Because the two might diverge enormously.

---

# 18. We already have evidence of exactly that divergence

February:

> almost $1tn software/services market-value panic. citeturn0news138

Yet by late September 2026, research reported in the Washington Post found **no statistically significant rise in unemployment specifically among young graduates seeking AI-vulnerable occupations**, despite a 7.3% graduate unemployment rate for the cohort studied. citeturn0news135

And just three days ago, Accenture's stronger outlook produced a **22% share-price jump**, while several IT-services peers rose sharply, partly easing AI-disruption fears. citeturn0news132

So even within 2026:

```text
AI WILL DESTROY SOFTWARE
        ↓
market panic
        ↓
new evidence
        ↓
AI integration demand strong
        ↓
market reassessment
```

**That itself looks like an expectations cycle.**

It does not yet prove a labour-market revolution.

---

# 19. Now the replay-history mode

This is the most important improvement.

The model gets a switch:

```text
MODE =
HISTORY_REPLAY
or
AI_SIMULATION
```

### Replay 1 — 1980/81

Feed only information available at shock onset:

```text
inflation
interest-rate shock
oil
sector structure
debt
employment
trade
productivity
government balance
```

Do **not** tell it what subsequently happened.

Predict:

```text
GDP Q+1 ... Q+20
unemployment Q+1 ... Q+20
inflation
consumption
investment
government deficit
sector employment
```

Compare with actual.

---

# 20. Replay 2 — 2008

Give it pre-crisis:

```text
housing
credit
household debt
bank exposure
construction employment
manufacturing
exports
interest rates
fiscal position
```

Then inject the financial shock.

The model must reproduce:

### US

deep contraction + ~10% unemployment.

### UK

deep contraction + slow GDP recovery.

### India

**slowdown but not equivalent contraction.**

If our equations make India collapse like the UK:

# Model fails.

That's an excellent validation test.

---

# 21. Replay 3 — 2020

Give it 2019 economic structure.

Then:

```text
contact-sector activity shock
mobility shock
supply restrictions
```

Run first:

### No government remedy.

Then actual policy:

```text
US transfers/support
UK furlough
India fiscal/credit/liquidity
central-bank response
```

Compare both.

That tells us whether our fiscal/monetary transmission mechanism is credible.

---

# 22. We score the replay mathematically

For GDP:

\[
RMSE_{GDP}
=
\sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum(\hat GDP_t-GDP_t)^2}
\]

For unemployment:

\[
RMSE_U
=
\sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum(\hat U_t-U_t)^2}
\]

Also:

- turning-point error,
- peak unemployment error,
- trough GDP error,
- recovery-time error,
- inflation error,
- fiscal-deficit error,
- sector-employment error.

Then create:

## Historical Replay Score

Not one magic number only—we retain the component errors.

---

# 23. More importantly — train on one crisis, test on another

Otherwise we can cheat accidentally.

For example:

```text
CALIBRATE:
1980 + 2008

BLIND TEST:
2020
```

Then:

```text
CALIBRATE:
1980 + 2020

BLIND TEST:
2008
```

Then:

```text
CALIBRATE:
2008 + 2020

BLIND TEST:
1980
```

And across countries:

```text
fit US
→ test UK/India

fit UK
→ test US/India
```

If it only reproduces the historical event whose parameters we fitted:

> **we have curve-fitting, not an economic model.**

---

# 24. Then AI mode uses the SAME equations

This is crucial.

We must not invent special AI equations just to produce an exciting answer.

Replace historical shock with:

\[
AIShock_i
=
Exposure_i
\times Adoption_i
\times ProductivityGain_i
\times Substitutability_i
\]

Then follow the exact same economy:

```text
AI productivity
       ↓
labour hours/unit ↓
       ↓
cost ↓
       ↓
price/profit split
       ↓
employment response
       ↓
wages
       ↓
household income
       ↓
consumption
       ↓
business revenue
       ↓
investment
       ↓
tax
       ↓
government balance
       ↓
borrowing/rates
       ↓
SECOND ROUND
```

Plus:

```text
new demand
new sectors
worker transition
capital ownership
exports/imports
```

---

# 25. And there should NOT be one AI forecast

We need scenarios.

| Scenario | AI adoption | Productivity | Labour displacement | New demand | Surplus distribution |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| **Slow augmentation** | slow | medium | low | medium | broad |
| **Productivity boom** | fast | high | medium | high | broad |
| **Corporate automation** | fast | high | high | medium | capital-heavy |
| **Demand crisis** | very fast | high | very high | slow | concentrated |
| **New-sector explosion** | fast | very high | high initially | **very high** | mixed |

Then run each through:

🇺🇸 US  
🇬🇧 UK  
🇮🇳 India.

They should respond differently because their economies are different.

---

# 26. India may actually be the most interesting AI experiment

Why?

Because the previous technology wave created:

```text
Western demand
      ↓
digitisable work
      ↓
telecommunications
      ↓
wage arbitrage
      ↓
Indian IT/BPO employment
```

AI attacks precisely:

> **digitisable cognitive work.**

So India could face:

```text
AI ↓ cost of Western domestic production
      ↓
offshoring advantage ↓
```

BUT simultaneously:

```text
AI ↓ cost per Indian engineer
      ↓
Indian engineer output ↑↑
      ↓
Indian firms can sell much more sophisticated output
```

Two opposing forces.

That cannot be answered with:

> “AI will destroy Indian IT.”

It has to be simulated.

---

# 27. And there is a third possibility

Something analogous to what happened after previous abstraction jumps.

Instead of:

```text
1 engineer = £100k software output
```

AI might produce:

```text
1 engineer + agents
=
£1m software output
```

Then if global software demand increases more than tenfold:

**employment need not fall.**

If demand only doubles:

employment falls substantially.

So the key elasticity is:

\[
\boxed{
\text{Demand growth relative to productivity growth}
}
\]

That may be one of the most important variables in the entire AI-employment debate.

---

# 28. The model we actually need

I would now define the system as **seven interacting engines**:

```text
┌──────────────────────┐
│ 1. PEOPLE            │
│ population/labour    │
│ skills/wages/hours   │
└──────────┬───────────┘
           ↕
┌──────────────────────┐
│ 2. INDUSTRIES        │
│ output/productivity  │
│ jobs/profits/prices  │
└──────────┬───────────┘
           ↕
┌──────────────────────┐
│ 3. HOUSEHOLDS        │
│ income/debt/saving   │
│ consumption          │
└──────────┬───────────┘
           ↕
┌──────────────────────┐
│ 4. FINANCE           │
│ credit/rates/assets  │
│ investment           │
└──────────┬───────────┘
           ↕
┌──────────────────────┐
│ 5. GOVERNMENT        │
│ tax/spend/debt       │
│ transfers/interest   │
└──────────┬───────────┘
           ↕
┌──────────────────────┐
│ 6. EXTERNAL WORLD    │
│ trade/FX/capital     │
│ offshoring           │
└──────────┬───────────┘
           ↕
┌──────────────────────┐
│ 7. TECHNOLOGY        │
│ adoption/productivity│
│ substitution/new need│
└──────────────────────┘
```

Then **history replay validates the connections**.

AI is merely a new input into Engine 7.

---

# 29. This changes my position again

I am now less interested in asking:

> “How many jobs can AI technically perform?”

That's not the economic question.

The historical evidence is pushing me toward:

\[
\boxed{
EmploymentEffect
\approx
ProductivityEffect
-
DemandExpansion
-
NewSectorCreation
-
WorkingTimeReduction
-
WorkerReallocation
}
\]

with distribution, trade and government modifying every term.

That equation isn't literally the final econometric equation yet—but **conceptually that's where the missing answer lives.**

And this explains your repeated objection to the current AI discussion.

People are measuring mostly the **first term**:

> productivity/substitution.

History says the outcome is determined by **the entire right-hand side**.

---

## What I would freeze now

I would **not build the simulator yet**.

The next research object should be one master historical panel:

**US 1929–2026 + UK 1948–2026 + India 1950/51–2026**, annual for the long history and quarterly wherever reliable, with sector GDP/employment, labour force, wages/income, consumption, investment, government tax/spend/debt/interest, inflation, trade, technology/work-method markers and every major recession.

Then annotate each transition:

**5 years before → shock → trough → policy → 5 years after → 10 years after.**

Only after that dataset is internally reconciled should we implement **History Replay**. Otherwise we'd merely encode today's assumptions into equations and congratulate ourselves when they reproduce the assumptions.

The February 2026 episode gives us a particularly useful current benchmark: **nearly $1 trillion of market-value fear about AI disruption** occurred before corresponding evidence of economy-wide AI unemployment existed. citeturn0news138turn0news135 That is precisely why our eventual model should keep **technology capability, market expectation, actual adoption, productivity and realised employment displacement as five separate variables.**

items.snippet:
A significant selloff has struck global software and services stocks, erasing nearly $1 trillion in market value as investors react to growing fears that artificial intelligence (AI) could pose an existential threat to traditional software firms. Triggered by a new legal tool plug-in from Anthropic’s Claude large language model, which targets core enterprise functions like legal, sales, and data analysis, concerns have escalated that AI is aggressively encroaching on high-value application areas.

The S&P 500 software and services index has dropped for six consecutive sessions, totaling a 13% decline and bringing its fall to 26% from its October peak. Major firms including Thomson Reuters, MSCI, and Relx have suffered sharp losses, as have asset managers such as Apollo, Blackstone, and KKR due to fears of potential credit risk tied to the ailing tech sector.

Comparisons are being drawn to Amazon’s disruptive market transformation, though analysts caution that AI's success depends on access to specialized data. While some warn of long-term labor and valuation risks, others believe the market reaction is overblown, noting AI could ultimately enhance efficiency and margins for software firms. Nvidia’s CEO called replacing software with AI “illogical,” suggesting the panic may be premature.
items.title: Selloff wipes out nearly $1 trillion from software and services stocks as investors debate AI's existential threat

items.snippet: A new study from two UCLA professors finds that concerns over artificial intelligence eliminating job opportunities for recent college graduates may be premature. According to the research, the unemployment rate for 22- to 25-year-old graduates during the summer months of June through August 2026 stood at 7.3%. While slightly higher than the same period in the previous year, this figure falls within normal variability. Importantly, the study found no statistically significant increase in unemployment for graduates seeking roles considered vulnerable to AI disruption, such as customer service or computer programming. Additionally, a broader measure of unemployment—those graduates who want jobs but aren’t actively job hunting, termed "sidelined unemployment"—did not show a significant AI-related impact either. The findings provide early insights into the labor market effects of AI on the graduating class of 2026, the first cohort to have access to ChatGPT during their college years.
items.title: Is AI killing jobs for college grads? Not yet, new study says.

items.snippet:
Accenture's shares rose by 22%, marking their best performance ever, after the company projected stronger-than-expected annual revenue growth, easing investor concerns about AI-led disruptions in the IT services sector. The optimistic outlook reflects increased demand from businesses seeking external partners to automate tasks and integrate AI technologies. This positive sentiment uplifted peer stocks, including Cognizant (up 8%) and IBM (up 3%), as well as Indian firms Wipro and Infosys (up 6-7%).

Accenture anticipates 3% to 6% annual revenue growth for fiscal 2027, exceeding analysts' average expectations. CEO Julie Sweet announced plans to invest approximately $5 billion in acquisitions to support growth, following cybersecurity deals totaling $4.18 billion in June. Despite pricing pressures due to clients seeking AI-related cost savings, Accenture reported a 4% rise in quarterly bookings to $22.17 billion, with consulting revenues up 7% to $9.28 billion. Total revenue hit $18.68 billion, surpassing estimates. Additionally, Accenture has partnered with Anthropic to invest at least $1 billion each over five years to enhance AI safety and testing.
items.title: Accenture's forecast eases AI disruption fears, lifts battered IT services stocks
