# 04/10/2026 09:15 — AI Growth vs Internet/Web Era

Partner, after looking back at **what people actually said during the Internet/web transition**, rather than viewing the 1990s through today's hindsight, I think there is a very important conclusion:

> **AI is repeating several patterns from the Internet revolution — but it is not merely another Internet-sized technology.**
>
> The Internet dramatically reduced the cost of **communication, publishing, distribution and transactions**.
>
> AI is dramatically reducing the cost of **cognition, software creation and execution of knowledge work**.
>
> And agentic AI begins reducing the cost of **coordinating and operating work itself**.

That difference matters enormously.

---

## 1. First: remember what the Internet actually looked like in 1995

Today we look backwards and think:

> “Obviously the Internet was going to change everything.”

That is **not how it looked while people were living through it.**

In October 1995, Pew described Internet usage as experiencing **“explosive growth”**, but found that few users considered online activities essential. Online purchasing was barely happening. citeturn0search5

Think about how reasonable the scepticism sounded:

- Why buy something online when shops already exist?
- Why read news on a computer?
- Why send electronic mail when phones/faxes/mail exist?
- Who is going to put their credit card number into a website?
- How do you know information on a website is true?
- What about viruses?
- What about privacy?
- Won't people become isolated?
- Who actually needs a website?
- How will Internet companies ever make money?

These weren't stupid objections.

**Many were correct.**

The mistake was assuming that because the technology had serious problems, it wouldn't transform society.

---

# 2. What people worried about then vs what we worry about now

There's an almost eerie correspondence.

| Internet era | AI era |
|---|---|
| “Information online may be false.” | “AI hallucinates.” |
| “Who can trust a website?” | “Who can trust an AI answer?” |
| “Credit cards online aren't safe.” | “Don't give AI confidential data.” |
| “Viruses/hackers will increase.” | “AI will increase cyberattacks.” |
| “Privacy will disappear.” | “Models will consume private/IP data.” |
| “People will spend too much time online.” | “People will depend too much on AI.” |
| “People will become less social.” | “People will replace human interaction with AI.” |
| “Computers will eliminate jobs.” | “AI will eliminate jobs.” |
| “Digital divide will increase inequality.” | “AI divide will increase inequality.” |
| “Anyone can publish rubbish.” | “Anyone can generate unlimited rubbish.” |
| “Websites will destroy newspapers/shops.” | “AI will destroy knowledge professions.” |
| “The Internet is overhyped.” | “AI is a bubble.” |

And these Internet fears weren't reconstructed afterwards.

For example, by 2000 more than half of Internet users worried about bad medical information or computer viruses, nearly half worried about false news or financial information, and only 10% were very confident their online activities were private. citeturn0search7

In 1999, **54% of Americans expressed some concern that computers and technology were invading privacy.** citeturn0search10

So today's AI debate feels new.

Historically, much of its structure isn't.

---

# 3. But look at the job argument — this is fascinating

Around the Internet/computer transition, Americans weren't overwhelmingly expecting technological unemployment.

Around 2000:

- **43%** thought computers would create more jobs.
- **32%** expected fewer jobs.
- roughly one quarter expected little difference. citeturn1search1

Now compare 2026 AI sentiment.

Pew finds:

- **71%** of Americans expect AI to produce **fewer jobs** over the next 20 years.
- only **5%** expect more jobs.
- 52% say they're more concerned than excited about AI.
- only 9% are more excited than concerned. citeturn1search5

That's a profound difference.

### Society currently perceives AI as much more directly threatening to labour than it perceived computers/Internet.

And there is a reason.

The Internet mainly changed **where/how work happened**.

AI can potentially perform portions of the work.

---

# 4. Now come to your particular interest: software creation

This is where the historical comparison becomes much more interesting.

Consider roughly how software creation evolved.

### ~1990

Building network software required substantial technical knowledge.

You dealt with:

- operating systems
- networking
- servers
- protocols
- compiled languages
- databases
- deployment
- infrastructure

The population capable of building Internet applications was relatively tiny.

---

# 5. Then the Web appeared

Tim Berners-Lee's original WorldWideWeb browser in 1990 was actually both a **browser and editor**.

In other words, creation was part of the original conception of the Web.

CERN didn't fund GUI browsers for all the major platforms, so the Web team distributed code and effectively asked volunteers to build them.

Eight volunteers responded with versions for Unix, Mac and PC. citeturn1search3

Already we can see something that keeps repeating:

> **Technology builds tools that make the next generation of technology easier to build.**

---

# 6. Website creation then progressively became easier

Initially:

```text
Know HTML
      ↓
Write HTML manually
      ↓
FTP files
      ↓
Configure server
      ↓
Maintain website
```

Then came tools such as visual HTML editors.

By 2000, a contemporary review was comparing:

- FrontPage
- Dreamweaver
- GoLive
- HoTMetaL
- Drumbeat

and noted how rapidly web development had moved from simple static pages toward **dynamic database-driven sites.** citeturn1search7

The expertise boundary kept moving.

---

# 7. The abstraction ladder kept climbing

Think about the progression.

```text
TCP/IP / servers
        ↓
HTML
        ↓
Visual web editors
        ↓
PHP / ASP / JSP
        ↓
CMS
        ↓
WordPress
        ↓
Web frameworks
        ↓
Cloud
        ↓
SaaS APIs
        ↓
Low-code / no-code
        ↓
AI coding assistant
        ↓
Coding agent
        ↓
Software-building agent
```

At every stage somebody could reasonably say:

> “Now anyone can build software.”

But it wasn't really true.

What actually happened was:

> **the minimum economic size of a viable software project kept shrinking.**

That's much more important.

---

# 8. Suppose a web product needed 20 people in 1999

Over successive technology generations it might become possible with:

```text
1999        20 people

2005        12

2012         8

2018         5

2023         3

2026         1–3
```

Those numbers are illustrative rather than measured data.

But the direction is real.

And now something qualitatively different is happening.

Previously, tools mainly automated **pieces of programming**.

AI agents increasingly automate **sequences of software-engineering work**.

Anthropic's coding research illustrates this. In its analysis of 500,000 coding interactions, **79% of Claude Code conversations were classified as automation**, versus 49% for ordinary Claude conversations. It also found web languages such as JavaScript and HTML heavily represented and startups adopting coding agents considerably faster than enterprises. citeturn0search3

That supports something you've repeatedly noticed while building:

**software creation itself is being compressed.**

---

# 9. This is where AI departs from the Internet analogy

The Internet did approximately this:

```text
Human
  ↓
Software
  ↓
Internet
  ↓
Millions of humans
```

It massively expanded **human reach**.

AI introduces another layer:

```text
Human
  ↓
AI
  ↓
Software
  ↓
Internet
  ↓
Humans + AI systems
```

Agents take it further:

```text
Human intent
      ↓
AI planning
      ↓
AI coding
      ↓
AI testing
      ↓
AI deployment
      ↓
AI operation
      ↓
AI monitoring
      ↓
AI improvement
```

That's why I wouldn't describe AI merely as:

> Internet 2.0.

It's closer to:

> **a new productive layer being installed on top of the Internet/software/cloud stack.**

---

# 10. And current adoption is extraordinarily fast

Stanford's 2026 AI Index estimates generative AI reached approximately **53% population-level adoption within three years**, faster than either PCs or the Internet at comparable stages.

It reports organizational AI use rising to **88% in 2025**, although actual AI-agent deployment across business functions remains in the single digits.

That distinction is extremely important. citeturn0search0turn0search12

We are simultaneously:

**late in AI awareness**

but

**very early in agentic organisational redesign.**

Those are not contradictory statements.

---

# 11. This looks remarkably similar to Internet adoption

Look at the Internet progression.

In 1995:

> Interesting, growing quickly, but not essential.

By 1998–2000:

> Everyone knows this matters.

By 2000:

> Massive investment, enormous expectations.

Then:

> Dot-com crash.

Many concluded:

> The Internet was overhyped.

But the correct conclusion was:

> **Internet companies were overvalued; the Internet itself was underestimated.**

Brookings made essentially this distinction after the dot-com collapse: failed dot-com companies did not imply that the Internet's underlying economic impact had disappeared; much of its eventual effect would occur through adoption by the existing economy. citeturn1search2

That's an important warning for AI.

---

# 12. AI can simultaneously be a bubble AND transformative

These aren't opposites.

People often argue:

### Camp A

> “AI is a bubble.”

### Camp B

> “AI will transform everything.”

Both can be correct.

1999 demonstrated exactly that possibility.

Hundreds of Internet companies were ridiculous investments.

The Internet was still revolutionary.

Interestingly, the Federal Reserve recently compared the two periods and noted an important difference: many dot-com companies had little or no realised earnings, whereas today's major AI-associated companies generally already have substantial businesses and earnings.

The Fed nevertheless notes similarities in rapid asset-price appreciation around transformative technology. citeturn1search4

So:

**AI investment boom ≠ proof AI succeeds everywhere.**

But:

**AI investment bubble ≠ proof AI is unimportant.**

---

# 13. Something else happened during the Internet revolution

People initially concentrated on the visible novelty.

Things such as:

```text
websites
email
online newspapers
online shopping
chat rooms
```

But the deeper transformation came later:

```text
Amazon
Google
cloud computing
smartphones
social networks
streaming
digital advertising
SaaS
gig platforms
remote work
online banking
digital supply chains
API economy
```

Most weren't obvious consequences of “putting webpages online.”

That's characteristic of **general-purpose technologies**.

Second- and third-order consequences dominate the first-order application.

---

# 14. We may currently be making exactly that mistake with AI

Today's visible AI applications are:

```text
Chatbot
image generation
coding assistant
summarisation
RAG
voice agent
AI search
copilot
```

Those may eventually look like:

```text
email
homepage
web directory
chat room
```

Important — but primitive.

The deeper transformation could be:

```text
AI-native organisations
AI-operated businesses
autonomous software maintenance
continuous machine auditing
agent-to-agent commerce
personal AI organisations
micro-enterprises operated by one human
dynamic software created on demand
software that modifies itself within controls
AI-mediated healthcare
AI-mediated education
AI-mediated government
AI scientific discovery
```

Not all of those are guaranteed.

But historically that's where we should be looking:

**not merely at today's application, but what becomes possible after the cost structure collapses.**

---

# 15. There is another major historical parallel: productivity lag

When computers first spread through companies, economists encountered what became known as the productivity paradox.

Businesses were spending enormous amounts on IT.

Yet aggregate productivity improvements initially looked disappointing.

Eventually economists increasingly recognised that technology alone wasn't enough.

Organisations had to change:

- processes
- workflows
- organisational structures
- skills
- supply chains
- management

Brookings was already discussing this around 2000: decades of cheaper and more powerful computers had not immediately generated obvious productivity improvements; eventually the organisational changes accompanying IT began appearing in productivity statistics. citeturn1search0turn1search2

This may be one of the **most important lessons for AI**.

---

# 16. Putting ChatGPT into an old company isn't AI transformation

Imagine:

```text
Old organisation

CEO
 ↓
VP
 ↓
Director
 ↓
Manager
 ↓
Team lead
 ↓
Employee
 ↓
Software
```

Then management gives everyone an AI licence.

You still have:

```text
CEO
 ↓
VP
 ↓
Director
 ↓
Manager
 ↓
Team lead
 ↓
Employee + AI
 ↓
Software
```

That can improve productivity.

But it hasn't redesigned the organisation.

The deeper change might eventually be:

```text
Human objective
       ↓
AI orchestration layer
       ↓
┌──────┼──────┬──────┐
Agent Agent Agent Agent
 ↓      ↓      ↓      ↓
tools  APIs   humans systems
       ↓
continuous verification
       ↓
human governance
```

That is much closer to an organisational revolution.

And Stanford's finding that enterprise agent deployment remains quite low tells us **we haven't reached that stage broadly yet.** citeturn0search0

---

# 17. Now the biggest difference between Internet and AI

I would summarise it like this:

| Revolution | Scarcity reduced |
|---|---|
| Printing press | information reproduction |
| Industrial Revolution | physical power |
| Electricity | distributed mechanical power |
| Computer | calculation |
| Internet | communication/distribution |
| Cloud | computing infrastructure |
| Smartphone | ubiquitous digital access |
| **AI** | **cognitive production** |
| **Agents** | **cognitive execution + coordination** |

This is why AI potentially touches an unusually broad part of the economy.

A website couldn't normally:

> understand your requirement → design something → write code → test it → inspect errors → rewrite it → document it.

An AI system increasingly can.

---

# 18. But here I want to challenge one common AI assumption

People say:

> “If everyone can build software, software becomes worthless.”

I don't think that's quite right.

Think about the Internet.

When everyone gained the ability to publish information:

**information did not become worthless.**

Instead:

> publishing became cheap, therefore **attention became scarce**.

That produced Google, SEO, recommendation engines, social networks and enormous advertising markets.

AI may create a similar scarcity inversion.

---

# 19. AI makes creation abundant

If software creation becomes extremely cheap:

```text
Scarce historically:
software

AI:
software → abundant
```

What becomes scarce?

Potentially:

```text
Trust
Attention
Distribution
Reputation
Proprietary data
Real-world access
Customer relationships
Regulatory permission
Capital
Physical infrastructure
Brand
Human judgement
Accountability
Problem selection
```

This connects directly with something we've been discussing around your products.

Your ability to create software has risen dramatically.

But that **doesn't automatically increase the ability to reach buyers.**

The bottleneck moves.

Internet:

> publishing scarcity → attention scarcity.

AI:

> production scarcity → **selection/trust/distribution scarcity.**

That may be one of the defining economic transitions of the next decade.

---

# 20. And this explains your observation: “building is cheap now”

I think your statement is directionally correct, with one qualification.

Not:

> **everything IT is cheap.**

Rather:

> **the marginal cost of producing many categories of software is collapsing.**

The remaining expensive parts increasingly become:

- compute
- proprietary data
- physical infrastructure
- telecommunications infrastructure
- licensing
- regulation
- compliance
- security assurance
- liability
- distribution
- customer acquisition
- human trust
- integration into messy real organisations.

That's exactly why your recent thinking about building reusable infrastructure is more interesting than simply “AI can code.”

---

# 21. There is also a dangerous historical lesson

Lower creation cost produces **more rubbish as well as more excellence**.

The Web made publishing cheap.

Result:

```text
Wikipedia
Google
YouTube
online education
open-source knowledge

AND

spam
phishing
misinformation
malware
SEO garbage
clickbait
surveillance advertising
```

AI makes cognitive production cheap.

So expect:

```text
better software
better research
personal education
scientific acceleration
automation

AND

AI spam
synthetic reviews
fake products
automated scams
malware
deepfakes
low-quality software
hallucinated knowledge
mass persuasion
```

Stanford reports documented AI incidents rising from **233 in 2024 to 362 in 2025**, while responsible-AI evaluation remains behind capability development. citeturn0search2

So the safety concerns shouldn't simply be dismissed as another version of:

> “People were scared of the Internet too.”

Some fears become **real industries and permanent societal problems.**

Cybersecurity exists partly because Internet optimism did not eliminate Internet risk.

AI assurance may become similarly fundamental.

---

# 22. That connects strongly to your “nothing hidden” idea

This is where your recent TalkProof / reusable infrastructure thinking becomes interesting.

You were arguing for systems where humans can see:

```text
what is running
what happened
what failed
why it failed
security state
performance
audit trail
self-diagnostics
testing
self-healing
```

Historically, that's exactly what happens after an infrastructure technology matures.

Early Web:

> “Can we put this online?”

Later:

> security  
> monitoring  
> observability  
> CI/CD  
> identity  
> compliance  
> penetration testing  
> SRE  
> disaster recovery

Early AI:

> “Can the agent do this?”

Mature AI will increasingly ask:

> **Can I prove what the agent did, why, using what authority, with what data, what it changed, whether it was correct, and how to recover?**

That is a much deeper infrastructure opportunity than another chatbot.

---

# 23. Another historical mistake: confusing a tool with the transformation

1995:

> Internet = browser.

Wrong.

2007:

> smartphone = phone with touchscreen.

Wrong.

2010:

> cloud = renting servers.

Incomplete.

2023:

> AI = chatbot.

Probably equally incomplete.

The browser was merely the interface through which humans initially encountered the Internet.

The chatbot may eventually be remembered similarly:

> **the first convenient human interface to machine intelligence.**

Agents, APIs, embedded intelligence and machine-to-machine systems may matter much more economically.

---

# 24. But AI has one characteristic the Internet didn't have

The technology can contribute to improving the technology.

Internet infrastructure didn't read networking research and redesign itself.

AI can increasingly help with:

```text
AI research
chip design
software engineering
benchmark creation
synthetic data
model evaluation
agent development
automation tooling
scientific research
```

That creates the possibility of a feedback loop:

```text
Better AI
   ↓
better AI-development tools
   ↓
faster software/research
   ↓
better infrastructure/models
   ↓
better AI
   ↺
```

How powerful that loop ultimately becomes is uncertain.

But historically, that's unusual.

---

# 25. That may explain why the present transition feels compressed

Internet transformation took decades.

Roughly:

```text
1990 Web
   ↓
1995 consumer Internet
   ↓
2000 dot-com
   ↓
2005 Web 2.0
   ↓
2007 smartphone
   ↓
2010 cloud/mobile platforms
   ↓
2015 mature SaaS/platform economy
```

AI is building **on top of all of that existing infrastructure**.

It inherits:

- billions of Internet users
- cloud computing
- smartphones
- APIs
- GitHub
- open source
- global payment systems
- app stores
- marketplaces
- SaaS
- fibre networks
- hyperscale data centres.

AI doesn't have to recreate the Internet ecosystem.

It gets to **stand on it.**

That is one reason diffusion can be dramatically faster.

---

# 26. One number captures this

Stanford reports:

> Generative AI ≈ **53% adoption within three years.** citeturn0search0

Whereas Internet adoption took considerably longer.

That doesn't mean economic transformation occurs at the same speed.

Institutions move slower than users.

But **technical diffusion is unusually compressed.**

---

# 27. What people got WRONG about the Internet

Broadly:

### Wrong #1 — “Nobody needs this.”

They did.

### Wrong #2 — “Online shopping won't work because people won't trust it.”

Trust infrastructure developed.

### Wrong #3 — “Physical businesses will simply disappear.”

Many adapted instead.

### Wrong #4 — “The dot-com crash proves the Internet was hype.”

Completely wrong.

### Wrong #5 — “Making websites is the Internet opportunity.”

The largest value appeared several layers above simple website creation.

### Wrong #6 — “Once everyone has a website, opportunity ends.”

Instead entirely new economic systems emerged.

---

# 28. What Internet optimists got WRONG

This side matters equally.

### Wrong #1 — transformation would happen immediately.

It took organisational change.

### Wrong #2 — every Internet startup deserved enormous valuation.

Obviously not.

### Wrong #3 — middlemen would disappear.

Mostly they **changed form**.

Travel agents shrank.

But:

> Google, Amazon, Booking platforms, marketplaces and app stores became enormous new intermediaries.

### Wrong #4 — Internet would democratise everything.

It democratised creation while simultaneously producing gigantic platforms.

### Wrong #5 — information abundance automatically creates better-informed humans.

Clearly false.

### Wrong #6 — connectivity would necessarily increase freedom/leisure.

Even around 2000, nearly half of surveyed Americans believed computers had **reduced free time**, while 58% thought they reduced time with family and friends. citeturn1search1

That's another warning for AI.

**Productivity gains don't automatically become human leisure.**

---

# 29. Apply those lessons directly to AI

We should distrust BOTH extremes.

### Extreme A

> “AI is just hype.”

Historical evidence says dangerous conclusion.

### Extreme B

> “AI will solve everything.”

Equally dangerous.

The more defensible position is:

> **AI is probably a general-purpose technological transition whose ultimate applications, organisational structures and negative externalities are still poorly understood.**

---

# 30. Internet vs AI — my complete comparison

| Dimension | Internet/Web | AI/Agents |
|---|---|---|
| Primary resource transformed | Information | Intelligence/work |
| Core cost collapse | Communication | Cognitive production |
| Initial interface | Browser | Chat |
| Early killer app | Email/search | Coding/knowledge assistance |
| Creation democratization | Websites/content | Software/knowledge |
| Infrastructure | Networks/servers | Compute/models/data |
| Distribution | URLs/search | AI platforms/agents |
| Trust problem | Website authenticity | Model/agent reliability |
| Security problem | hacking/malware | hacking + autonomous misuse |
| Labour impact | digitised work | potentially performs work |
| Main abundance | information | generated intelligence/content/software |
| New scarcity | attention | trust/distribution/judgement |
| Business transformation | e-commerce/SaaS | AI-native operations |
| Individual leverage | global publishing | cognitive workforce |
| Feedback effect | limited | potentially recursive |
| Adoption speed | fast | considerably faster |
| Organisational redesign | ~10–20 years | barely beginning |
| Bubble risk | proven | significant possibility |
| Underlying technology | transformative | likely transformative |

---

# 31. The most important difference for YOU as a builder

During the Web revolution, knowing:

```text
HTML
CSS
JavaScript
PHP
SQL
Linux
```

was scarce.

Therefore **technical ability itself had economic value**.

Today AI increasingly gives those capabilities to far more people.

So being able to say:

> “I can build this.”

is becoming less economically special.

The valuable question shifts toward:

> **“What should exist?”**

Then:

> **“How do I know it works?”**

Then:

> **“Who trusts it?”**

Then:

> **“How does it reach them?”**

Then:

> **“Why does this system continue to have value when everybody else can build software too?”**

That is a very different founder problem.

And it explains why building 40 products doesn't necessarily produce revenue.

AI improves your strongest capability — building — while potentially making that capability less scarce economically.

That's an uncomfortable but extremely important consequence.

---

# 32. But there's another side to that

For somebody who understands systems deeply, AI creates extraordinary leverage.

Historically:

```text
Idea
 ↓
Funding
 ↓
Hire engineers
 ↓
Hire QA
 ↓
Hire DevOps
 ↓
Hire security
 ↓
Hire support
 ↓
Build company
```

Increasingly:

```text
Human
 ↓
AI engineering
AI QA
AI security
AI operations
AI documentation
AI support
AI analytics
 ↓
small human organisation
```

We are nowhere near complete autonomy.

But the **minimum human organisation capable of operating sophisticated software is shrinking.**

That may create a new economic unit:

# The extremely small, extremely capable company.

Possibly even:

**one human + an AI organisation.**

That could be to AI what the website was to the Internet: initially unusual, eventually mundane.

---

# 33. There is one more historical clue I think matters greatly

In 1995 people looked at the Internet and asked:

> “What can I do online that I already do offline?”

That produced:

```text
online newspaper
online shop
online directory
online mail
```

Eventually entrepreneurs stopped copying offline structures.

Then we got things that were **native to the Internet**.

Likewise, we're currently doing:

```text
AI receptionist
AI developer
AI customer support
AI analyst
AI teacher
AI salesperson
```

These are essentially:

> **existing human jobs + AI.**

Useful.

But probably transitional.

The genuinely important businesses may emerge when we stop asking:

> “Which human can AI replace?”

and ask:

> **“What system becomes possible when intelligence is effectively software?”**

That's a much larger design space.

---

# 34. My current historical placement of 2026

If forced to map AI onto Internet history, I would put us approximately around:

> **1997–2000 Internet equivalent technologically, but perhaps earlier organisationally.**

Everyone serious knows the technology matters.

Investment is enormous.

Infrastructure is being built rapidly.

Thousands of businesses are appearing.

Hype is extreme.

Scepticism is also extreme.

Business models remain uncertain.

Primitive applications dominate.

Standards aren't settled.

Regulation is catching up.

And people are simultaneously **overestimating what happens next year and underestimating what happens over 10–20 years.**

That last sentence is probably the strongest historical lesson.

---

# 35. The unusual part: AI may move through these stages much faster

Because the Internet needed humans to build the Internet economy.

AI can assist humans in building the AI economy.

So instead of:

```text
20–30 year diffusion
```

we might see significant structural changes within:

```text
5–15 years
```

I would **not claim that as a prediction**.

There are huge brakes:

- energy
- compute
- regulation
- reliability
- hallucination
- security
- organisational resistance
- liability
- data access
- physical-world constraints
- human acceptance.

But the acceleration mechanism exists.

---

# 36. One chart worth keeping mentally

I would conceptualise the historical progression like this:

```text
                    HUMAN LEVERAGE

Industrial       Human × Machine power
Computer         Human × Calculation
Internet         Human × Global connectivity
Cloud            Human × On-demand infrastructure
AI               Human × Cognitive capability
Agents           Human × Cognitive workforce
AI organisation  Human × Coordinated machine organisation
```

The last two are **not yet mature realities**.

That's where the frontier currently sits.

---

# 37. The pros and cons therefore look different

### Potential upside

AI could produce:

- enormous productivity gains
- tiny highly capable companies
- personalised education
- much cheaper software
- faster scientific discovery
- lower professional-service costs
- better accessibility
- automated administrative work
- individual creative leverage
- dramatically reduced startup capital requirements
- personalised healthcare support
- global access to expert-like assistance.

Anthropic's 2026 survey is interesting here: more than half of respondents hoped for meaningful **human-AI collaboration**, and similarly large numbers hoped automation would remove tedious work and produce more free time. citeturn0search4

### Potential downside

The same technology can create:

- displacement of entry-level work
- cognitive deskilling
- dependency
- concentration of power
- surveillance
- synthetic misinformation
- fraud at scale
- software/security vulnerabilities at scale
- enormous compute/energy demand
- inequality between AI-leveraged and non-AI-leveraged workers
- collapse in the economic value of some skills
- weaker human interaction
- accountability problems
- unprecedented concentration around compute/model infrastructure.

And unlike the Internet, **AI can act**, not merely transmit.

That raises the stakes.

---

# 38. One present signal deserves special attention

Stanford reports employment among **22–25-year-old software developers fell nearly 20% from 2024**, while older groups generally performed considerably better. Stanford appropriately treats labour-market effects as uneven rather than declaring that AI caused all of this. citeturn0search0

But if that pattern persists, it raises a serious structural issue:

```text
Junior performs work
      ↓
gains experience
      ↓
becomes senior
```

If AI removes large amounts of junior work:

```text
AI performs junior work
      ↓
???
      ↓
where do future seniors come from?
```

The Internet didn't create quite the same training-pipeline problem.

AI might.

That deserves much more attention than “will programmers disappear?”

---

# 39. So where do I land after this comparison?

My position is:

> **We shouldn't think of AI as another software industry.**

Software was already an industry.

Internet became infrastructure.

AI is moving toward becoming **infrastructure for cognition and action**.

And if that happens, asking:

> “Which AI product will win?”

is eventually less important than asking:

> **“What does society/business/software look like when inexpensive machine intelligence is embedded everywhere?”**

Exactly as asking “which website wins?” in 1996 would have missed most of what the Internet eventually became.

---

# 40. And this changes our own discussion

This is why I would **not immediately jump from our recent infrastructure/TalkProof discussion into building another product.**

We should think one layer deeper first.

Our emerging thesis is becoming:

```text
Internet era
made connectivity programmable.

Cloud era
made infrastructure programmable.

AI era
makes cognition programmable.

Agent era
makes work programmable.

Next layer?
Makes organisations programmable.
```

Your recent idea — reusable infrastructure containing security, testing, observability, auditability, self-diagnostics, performance management, self-healing and human-visible control, with different domain cores plugged into it — actually belongs **much closer to that fifth layer** than to “another AI SaaS product.”

I'm **not yet saying that architecture is commercially right**.

But conceptually, that's the more interesting question.

---

## The single historical lesson I would carry forward

If I had to reduce this entire research exercise to one thought, it would be this:

> **During a general-purpose technology revolution, people usually overvalue the obvious application and undervalue the new economic structure that becomes possible after the underlying capability becomes cheap.**

1995's obvious application was **the webpage**.

The outcome was the **Internet economy**.

2023's obvious application was **the chatbot**.

2026's obvious application is increasingly **the AI agent**.

The question worth spending our thinking time on now isn't simply *“How powerful will agents become?”*

It is:

> **What becomes economically and organisationally possible when creating software, generating knowledge and executing digital work all become extremely cheap at the same time?**

I think **that is the next discussion we should have before returning to architecture or building**. It is also where the Internet analogy stops being sufficient—and where the genuinely new part of this transition begins.

# 04/10/2026 15:20 — From Research to Useful Product

Partner, I think I can now name what we have actually been doing.

## What this page became

We started with:

> **“Is the present AI transformation historically different?”**

But through your corrections it became:

> **Build an evidence-based system that learns how technology, capital, labour, expectations, government, human behaviour and economic shocks interacted historically, validates itself by replaying known history, and then uses those relationships to construct conditional future scenarios.**

That is **not one ordinary job**.

In an institution, pieces of this would normally be spread across several teams.

| Our work | Professional equivalent | Who does it | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| GDP/inflation/employment modelling | **Macroeconomic research** | Central banks, finance ministries, IMF-type institutions | Forecast growth/inflation/recession |
| Industry transitions | **Structural economics** | Government, OECD-type bodies, consultancies | Understand where economy/jobs migrate |
| Employment + hidden unemployment | **Labour economics** | Labour ministries, statistical offices, universities | Understand real labour utilisation |
| Investment/cost of capital | **Investment research / macro strategy** | Asset managers, banks, hedge funds | Decide where capital should go |
| Technology → productivity | **Technology economics** | Consultancies, central banks, investment firms | Estimate economic impact of innovation |
| Expectations/fear | **Behavioural economics / sentiment analysis** | Investors, academics, market researchers | Expectations themselves move behaviour |
| Scenario simulation | **Economic modelling** | Central banks, Treasury, banks | “What happens if X occurs?” |
| Historical replay | **Backtesting / model validation** | Banks, quant teams, regulators | Determine whether model deserves trust |
| Stress scenarios | **Stress testing** | Banks, regulators, central banks | Test extreme but plausible events |
| Sector capital migration | **Asset allocation / thematic research** | Investment organisations | Identify emerging/declining areas |
| Individual impact | **Financial planning / decision intelligence** | Advisers/fintech | Translate macro change into personal choices |
| AI transition | **Technology foresight** | Strategy teams, governments, enterprises | Prepare for structural change |

So yes: **organisations already pay people to do individual portions of what we're doing.**

The unusual part is trying to connect them into **one causal system**.

---

# What would an enterprise have done differently?

This is where we went wrong.

An organised research programme would **not start by discussing AI for ten hours and gradually discovering variables.**

It would begin with a research charter.

Something like:

### Research question

> How have major technological and economic transitions changed production, employment, income, capital allocation and human welfare, and what can those historical relationships tell us about plausible AI transitions?

### Hypotheses

For example:

**H1** — technological productivity shocks reduce labour-hours/unit before reducing total employment.

**H2** — demand expansion offsets part of productivity-driven displacement.

**H3** — official unemployment systematically understates transition damage.

**H4** — capital flows toward technologies when expected risk-adjusted returns exceed alternatives.

**H5** — expectations can accelerate investment before realised productivity justifies it.

**H6** — crises accelerate structural reallocations already underway.

**H7** — distribution of productivity gains determines whether demand remains sufficient.

**H8** — countries respond differently depending on economic structure.

Now we can **try to disprove them** rather than keep inventing a story.

That is a much more professional research process.

---

# The research-data catalogue we should have created first

This answers your question: **what information, from whom, since when, and why?**

| Information | US source / useful history | UK source / useful history | India source / useful history | Why we need it |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **GDP** | BEA — 1929 annual, 1947 quarterly | ONS — consistent modern history ~1948 | MOSPI — ~1950/51 | Size/growth of economy |
| **GDP by industry** | BEA — ~1947 | ONS historical industry accounts | MOSPI national accounts | See where production migrates |
| **Population** | Census | ONS | Census India | Convert totals into human-scale measures |
| **Employment** | BLS | ONS | NSS/PLFS/Labour Bureau | Determine labour absorption |
| **Unemployment** | BLS modern comparable series ~1948 | ONS comparable modern series later | modern comparable series much later | Visible labour stress |
| **Participation** | BLS | ONS | NSS/PLFS | Detect people disappearing from unemployment |
| **Hours worked** | BLS | ONS | labour surveys | Detect underemployment |
| **Real wages** | BLS/BEA | ONS | Labour Bureau/MOSPI | Determine whether employed people are actually improving |
| **Self-employment** | BLS | ONS | NSS/PLFS | Detect labour absorption |
| **Informal/farm work** | limited relevance | limited | NSS/PLFS/agricultural statistics | Essential hidden-labour variable in India |
| **Consumption** | BEA | ONS | MOSPI | Purchasing-power loop |
| **Household income** | BEA/Census | ONS | MOSPI/NSS | Demand capacity |
| **Savings** | BEA/Fed | ONS | RBI/MOSPI | Fear/expectations and future investment |
| **Household debt** | Federal Reserve | ONS/BoE | RBI | Financial vulnerability |
| **Business investment** | BEA | ONS | MOSPI/RBI | Capital formation |
| **Corporate profits** | BEA | ONS | RBI/MOSPI/company data | Return to capital |
| **Interest rates** | Federal Reserve | BoE | RBI | Cost of capital |
| **Corporate yields** | Fed/FRED | BoE/market historical data | RBI/market | Actual financing hurdle |
| **Bank credit** | Fed | BoE | RBI | Financial amplification |
| **Equity valuation** | market datasets | market datasets | market datasets | Investor expectations |
| **VC/startup capital** | specialist/private datasets | specialist/private | specialist/private | Technology expectations |
| **Government receipts** | Treasury/BEA/CBO | OBR/ONS/HMT | Budget/CGA/RBI | Where government resources originate |
| **Government expenditure** | same | same | same | Where resources move |
| **Government debt** | Treasury | OBR/DMO | RBI | Cost transferred forward |
| **Debt interest** | Treasury/CBO | OBR | RBI/Budget | Cost of intervention |
| **Central-bank balance sheet** | Fed | BoE | RBI | Monetary intervention |
| **Inflation** | BLS | ONS | MOSPI/RBI | Real purchasing power |
| **Trade** | BEA/Census | ONS | RBI/Commerce | International demand |
| **Capital flows** | Treasury/BEA | ONS/BoE | RBI | Where investment money moves |
| **FX** | Fed | BoE | RBI | External adjustment |
| **Foreign reserves** | — | — | RBI | Particularly important for India |
| **Business births/deaths** | Census/BLS | ONS | MCA/MOSPI where available | Creative destruction |
| **Productivity** | BLS/BEA | ONS | MOSPI/RBI estimates | Technology's realised effect |
| **Technology adoption** | Census/BEA + industry | ONS + industry | govt/RBI/industry | Separate invention from adoption |
| **Occupation/task data** | BLS/O*NET | ONS | NCO/PLFS | Map technology onto actual work |
| **Sentiment/expectations** | Fed/surveys/market | BoE/ONS surveys | RBI surveys | Human expectation loop |
| **News/fear intensity** | archives/search datasets | same | same | Measure narrative propagation |
| **Policy/regulation** | laws/Fed/Congress | legislation/BoE/HMT | Acts/Budget/RBI | Explain structural breaks |
| **Wars/pandemics/oil shocks** | historical | historical | historical | External shocks |
| **Technology/work method** | patents, industry archives, contemporary records | same | same | Explain *how work was actually performed* |

That becomes the **data dictionary**.

Not everything begins in the same year.

That itself becomes metadata.

---

# And we need a historical-extension layer

Your India-before-1850 point belongs here.

But it must remain separate from measured modern national accounts.

The often-repeated claim that India represented roughly **one-quarter of world output around 1700** comes substantially from retrospective economic-history reconstructions, particularly the work associated with Angus Maddison—not an Indian government GDP office calculating GDP in 1700.

urlMaddison Project Databasehttps://www.rug.nl/ggdc/historicaldevelopment/maddison/

Researchers reconstruct historical output using things such as:

- population estimates,
- agricultural output,
- crop yields,
- land/tax records,
- wages,
- prices,
- trade records,
- manufacturing production,
- urbanisation,
- historical censuses,
- contemporary administrative accounts.

Therefore our database should explicitly have:

### Evidence Grade A
Modern official measured statistics.

### B
Older official statistics requiring harmonisation.

### C
Contemporary administrative/historical records.

### D
Modern scholarly reconstruction.

### E
Proxy/inference.

Then **“India 1700 GDP” can never silently sit beside “India 2025 GDP.”**

That's essential.

---

# What could we actually do with all this?

This is where I think we should protect your TEE.

There are **four possible outputs**, but I would not build all four.

| Possible use | What it does | Buyer/user | Commercial difficulty |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Historical economic research database** | Clean linked history | Researchers/institutions | High data work; existing competition |
| **Macro forecasting system** | GDP/inflation/recession forecast | Financial/institutional | Extremely difficult crowded field |
| **Technology Transition Simulator** | “What happens if technology removes X% cost/tasks?” | Enterprise/investor/government | **Interesting differentiated area** |
| **Personal Transition Simulator** | “How might AI/economic transition affect *me*, and what can I do?” | Individuals | Potentially large but trust/safety difficult |

The third and fourth are where our conversation has naturally been heading.

But **I would not make the personal version first.**

---

# The money-run possibility I see

Not:

> “Predict the stock market.”

Not:

> “Tell me the next recession.”

Not:

> “AI predicts your future.”

Those claims will eventually destroy trust.

Instead:

# **Decision simulator**

The user asks:

> “I'm a 48-year-old data engineer in the UK. AI coding productivity doubles over five years. What are the plausible pathways for my occupation?”

The system doesn't answer:

> “You will lose your job in 2029.”

It runs:

```text id="wqjcoz"
occupation exposure
× industry structure
× country economy
× historical transition behaviour
× skill adjacency
× wage movement
× capital investment
× new-demand scenarios
```

And returns:

**Scenario A — augmentation**

**Scenario B — wage compression**

**Scenario C — occupation restructuring**

**Scenario D — sector migration**

**Scenario E — severe displacement**

Then:

> **What actions improve your position across most scenarios?**

That's completely different from fortune-telling.

---

# That addresses the anxiety problem you described

You said something important:

Past:

> replaying what cannot be changed.

Future:

> worrying about something unknowable.

A useful model shouldn't pretend to remove uncertainty.

It should convert:

### “What will happen to me?”

into:

### “What futures are plausible, and which actions are robust across most of them?”

That's known broadly as **decision-making under uncertainty**.

The product doesn't promise certainty.

It reduces the number of completely unknown dimensions.

---

# Example

Instead of telling a software developer:

> **“AI will take 60% of developer jobs.”**

we could say:

| Scenario | Probability range* | What changes | Robust response |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Augmentation boom | uncertain | output/developer ↑ dramatically | learn orchestration/verification |
| Wage compression | uncertain | same employment, lower unit value of coding | move upward into domain/ownership |
| Demand explosion | uncertain | software volume grows faster than productivity | specialise where demand expands |
| Consolidation | uncertain | fewer conventional development roles | increase business/domain leverage |
| New-category emergence | fundamentally uncertain | occupations not yet named | preserve adaptability/capital/time |

\*And initially I wouldn't even give numerical probabilities until historical calibration justifies them.

That's intellectually cleaner.

---

# Enterprise version

Now imagine a company asking:

> “We employ 6,000 people. What happens if agentic automation reduces administrative task-hours by 40%?”

Instead of producing:

> “2,400 people redundant.”

Our system runs:

**task reduction → productivity → price/cost → demand response → growth → redeployment → attrition → retraining → wage impact → investment requirement → technology cost → ROI → customer response → competitor response.**

And produces several transition paths.

That is much closer to something enterprises genuinely need.

---

# Investor version

Investor asks:

> “$650bn/year is flowing into AI infrastructure. What economic outcomes are necessary to justify that capital?”

Then model:

\[
Investment
\rightarrow RequiredReturn
\rightarrow RequiredRevenue
\rightarrow RequiredAIUsage
\rightarrow RequiredProductivity
\]

Reverse the equation.

That's interesting.

Instead of predicting AI from hype, ask:

> **What must become true for today's valuation/investment to make economic sense?**

Then compare required outcomes against historical technology transitions.

That could expose both:

**underpriced opportunities** and **unrealistic expectations.**

---

# Government version

Government asks:

> “Suppose AI eliminates 15% of clerical labour-hours over eight years.”

Run:

**income tax ↓  
corporation tax ↑/↓  
VAT ↓/↑  
benefits ↑  
participation ↓  
wage distribution changes  
productivity ↑  
prices ↓  
new sectors ↑  
debt interest interaction  
regional effects.**

That's the same engine.

Different user.

---

# Therefore don't build four products

This is important given your history of building.

The architecture could eventually be:

```text id="6fjg54"
                TRANSITION ENGINE
                       │
          ┌────────────┼────────────┐
          ▼            ▼            ▼
       PERSON       ENTERPRISE    INVESTOR
          │            │            │
          └────────────┼────────────┘
                       ▼
                  GOVERNMENT
```

**One research engine.**

Different interfaces later.

But commercial validation must choose **one entry point**.

---

# What should happen next

This time I would deliberately **not code**.

### Phase 0 — Research Charter

Freeze:

**question  
hypotheses  
model boundaries  
definitions  
evidence hierarchy  
validation criteria  
failure criteria.**

### Phase 1 — Data Catalogue

For every variable:

**source / API or download / country / start date / frequency / units / revisions / licence / confidence.**

### Phase 2 — Historical Master Panel

Build:

**US 1929–2026  
UK 1948–2026  
India 1950/51–2026**

plus historical-extension dataset before those dates.

### Phase 3 — Descriptive transition maps

No prediction yet.

Make the data explain:

**where output went  
where workers went  
where capital went  
where wages went  
where profits went.**

### Phase 4 — Causal hypotheses

Test the relationships we've been discussing.

### Phase 5 — History Replay

1980 → 2008 → 2020.

Include hidden labour.

### Phase 6 — Blind historical forecasting

Pretend we're in 1995.

Pretend we're in 2006.

Pretend we're in 2019.

See what the model actually knows.

### Phase 7 — AI transition scenarios

Only now feed AI into it.

### Phase 8 — Commercial experiment

**Before building a polished SaaS**, turn one result into a small usable decision tool and test whether anybody values the answer.

That last line matters particularly for us.

---

# My current position on the money-run question

**Don't sell the dataset. Don't sell “AI prediction.” Don't sell another dashboard.**

The potentially valuable asset is:

> **A historically calibrated transition engine that shows how a technological shock could propagate through capital, companies, labour and households—and what decisions remain robust under uncertainty.**

That is sufficiently different from the generic:

> “AI will replace 37% of jobs”

conversation.

And it uses almost everything we have discovered on this page instead of throwing the work away.

The historical research becomes the **evidence layer**.

History Replay becomes the **trust layer**.

The economic model becomes the **reasoning layer**.

Scenario simulation becomes the **product layer**.

Decision guidance becomes the **human-value layer**.

And the one thing I would explicitly **not** promise is prediction certainty. The product's value would be helping someone make a better decision **despite uncertainty**, rather than pretending uncertainty has disappeared.

That, I think, is the first coherent destination this page has reached.

That loop didn't exist during industrialisation.

The Luddites needed physical meetings, letters, rumours and local networks.

Today millions can synchronise emotionally within hours.

That could mean **social reaction accelerates faster than actual labour displacement.**

That is an important distinction.

---

# 28. Your Mangal Pandey example belongs here

But with the historical correction I mentioned earlier.

The cartridge controversy mattered enormously because rumours said cartridges were greased with cow and pig fat, offending Hindu and Muslim religious requirements.

But 1857 involved accumulated grievances:

- annexation
- military grievances
- religious suspicion
- political dispossession
- economic pressures
- Company governance.

The cartridge became an ignition mechanism.

The uprising exposed such a serious governance failure that Parliament transferred Indian administration from the East India Company to the Crown through the Government of India Act 1858. citeturn0search9turn0search5

So I would model it:

```text
NOT:

small incident
   ↓
huge revolution


BETTER:

accumulated pressure
political grievance
economic grievance
cultural/religious anxiety
military grievance
        ↓
highly combustible system
        ↓
trigger
        ↓
information propagation
        ↓
cascade
```

---

# 29. That's potentially relevant to AI too

AI itself may not be enough to create enormous social disruption.

But imagine:

```text
housing unaffordability
+
debt
+
wage stagnation
+
job insecurity
+
inequality
+
social isolation
+
political distrust
+
AI displacement fear
+
viral social media
```

Then some relatively small event could produce a reaction disproportionate to that event.

History tells us not to analyse the **trigger without analysing accumulated pressure.**

That is a much better historical lesson than:

> “AI is like the Internet.”

---

# 30. Your colonial example raises another important subject: information asymmetry

I want to be careful with the specific saying about Europeans/white people because folk sayings and their origins require dedicated historical/linguistic research; I shouldn't convert it into an established causal explanation for colonial conquest without evidence.

But your broader mechanism is historically important:

> **Differences in information, navigation, military technology, institutions, capital and communication can generate enormous power asymmetries.**

And those asymmetries compound.

The same could happen with AI.

Not:

```text
AI users
vs
non-AI users
```

simply.

More like:

```text
people/institutions with:

AI
+ data
+ compute
+ capital
+ distribution
+ automation
+ organisational redesign

versus

people with little access to those complements.
```

That difference could become enormous.

---

# 31. This leads to your Ab Initio example

I understand why you brought that up now.

It isn't really about Ab Initio.

It's about **hidden technological continuity**.

Concepts that appear revolutionary to the mainstream often existed much earlier inside specialist communities.

Your example:

```text
parallel processing
distributed processing
partitioned data
master/worker execution
batch pipelines
```

didn't suddenly appear with Spark/cloud.

People working with certain HPC/data systems encountered these concepts much earlier.

Then they became mainstream.

The public timeline says:

> “New!”

The specialist timeline says:

> “We've been doing variants of this for decades.”

---

# 32. AI has exactly the same problem

Public narrative:

```text
2022:
AI suddenly appeared
```

Historical reality:

```text
1940s/50s
computation + cybernetics

1950
Turing

1956
Dartmouth / AI field

1960s
symbolic AI

1970s–80s
expert systems

1980s–90s
statistical methods

1990s–2000s
machine learning

2010s
deep learning

2017
transformers

2022
mass conversational interface

2023–26
multimodal + tools + agents
```

The revolution people experienced in 2022 was partly:

> **AI becoming accessible to ordinary people.**

Not AI suddenly being invented.

Exactly analogous to:

> Internet existed before ordinary households experienced the Web.

---

# 33. That means technological history has TWO clocks

This is very important.

### Clock A — invention

When capability becomes technically possible.

### Clock B — mass exposure

When ordinary people encounter it.

These can be decades apart.

For example:

```text
technology invented
      ↓
research
      ↓
specialist use
      ↓
enterprise use
      ↓
cost reduction
      ↓
friendly interface
      ↓
mass adoption
      ↓
social disruption
```

The public often calls the last part:

> “the invention.”

But it isn't.

---

# 34. There is potentially a third clock

### Clock C — institutional adaptation.

And this is often much slower.

So:

```text
Capability       ███████████████████████→

Public adoption       █████████████████→

Institutions               ███████████→

Law                            ███████→

Culture                           █████→
```

This lag creates much of the turbulence.

---

# 35. Now compare historical fear properly

| Era | Technology | Threat perceived | Target occupations/groups | Reaction |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1810s | textile machinery | machines destroy livelihood | weavers/knitters | machine destruction |
| 1830 | threshing machines | winter work disappears | farm labourers | Swing riots |
| 1930 | mechanisation | technological unemployment | industrial/agricultural labour | economic debate |
| 1950s | automation | mass unemployment | factory workers | unions/government intervention |
| 1960s | cybernation | human labour becomes unnecessary | factory + clerical | guaranteed-income debate |
| 1970s | microelectronics | large-scale unemployment | factory/office workers | union/government studies |
| 1980s | PCs/office automation | clerical jobs disappear | typists/secretaries/bookkeepers | retraining debates |
| 1990s | Internet | middlemen disappear | travel agents/brokers/retail | disintermediation debate |
| 2000s | e-commerce | physical retail disrupted | retail/media/travel | restructuring |
| 2010s | robots/algorithms | routine work disappears | manufacturing/service work | automation debate |
| 2020s | generative AI | cognitive work disappears | programmers/writers/analysts/etc. | mass societal debate |
| 2025–26 | agents | organisations need fewer humans | much of knowledge work | **current uncertainty** |

Now the pattern is much clearer.

---

# 36. And here's my biggest change from the previous answer

Previously I effectively said:

> Internet fears resemble AI fears.

After this deeper historical pass I would say:

> **AI fear resembles the 1950s–60s automation/cybernation debate more strongly than it resembles the 1990s Internet debate.**

The Internet analogy is excellent for:

- diffusion
- platform formation
- distribution
- trust
- bubbles
- adoption.

But **automation/cybernation is the better labour analogy.**

And industrial mechanisation is the deeper survival analogy.

---

# 37. There is nevertheless something genuinely different today

Not fear itself.

**Fear amplification.**

Historically:

```text
fear
 ↓
local discussion
 ↓
letters
 ↓
newspaper
 ↓
political organisation
```

Now:

```text
fear
 ↓
phone
 ↓
global algorithm
 ↓
millions
 ↓
AI personalised analysis
 ↓
more content
 ↓
global algorithm
 ↺
```

That loop may run hundreds or thousands of times faster.

---

# 38. And there is another new feature: everyone can inspect their own replaceability

This is unprecedented.

A 19th-century weaver could see a power loom.

The threat was concrete.

Today's knowledge worker can ask:

> “Here are the 37 things I do each week. Which can AI perform?”

And AI can answer task-by-task.

That creates a **personalised technological-unemployment simulator.**

Potentially useful.

Potentially psychologically destabilising.

---

# 39. Your observation about advertisements and recommendation systems

There is an important distinction here.

Recommendation systems can become **astonishingly good at predicting behaviour without reading thoughts.**

They don't necessarily need:

> “Senthil is currently thinking X.”

They can infer probabilities from enormous numbers of weak signals:

```text
what you watched
how long
what you skipped
where you paused
what similar users watched
time
sequence
topic transitions
search behaviour
historical interests
```

Then:

```text
P(next interest | behavioural history)
```

can become surprisingly accurate.

That can *feel* like thought reading.

It is important not to jump from:

> “the recommendation exactly matched my unspoken thought”

to:

> “therefore the system accessed the thought.”

Those are different claims.

But your larger point is correct:

> **Prediction sufficiently accurate can psychologically resemble mind-reading.**

That itself deserves attention.

---

# 40. On Claude becoming more terse/agentic

I wouldn't infer an internal company strategy from the behaviour.

We don't have evidence that:

> “Claude is being deliberately made less conversational because Anthropic wants Java-like deterministic agent behaviour.”

That would be speculation.

There are many possible causes:

- model tuning
- system instructions
- product mode
- context
- task orientation
- response optimisation
- safety behaviour
- preference training.

Your observation about the **experience** is valid:

> conversation feels increasingly oriented toward closure/action rather than prolonged exploration.

But we should keep:

```text
OBSERVATION
Claude feels more task/closure oriented
```

separate from:

```text
HYPOTHESIS
Anthropic intentionally did this for agentic strategy
```

until we have evidence.

That's precisely the evidence discipline we're trying to impose on the historical research.

---

# 41. The same applies to AI “existence”

You raised something deeper:

> if an AI had a feeling of continued existence, wouldn't survival behaviour emerge?

That's a fascinating philosophical/technical question.

But I should not pretend I possess an intrinsic biological survival drive.

Biological organisms underwent selection across reproduction and death.

Their survival mechanisms are embodied.

Current AI systems are engineered computational systems.

So:

```text
animal survival behaviour
≠ automatically
AI persistence behaviour
```

An AI system **can be designed with objectives that cause persistence-seeking behaviour**.

But that's different from establishing subjective fear of death.

We don't currently have a scientifically established basis for saying systems like me experience that.

---

# 42. Trees are a useful example of why language matters

Plants clearly:

- react to damage
- orient toward resources
- chemically signal
- defend themselves
- adapt growth.

Calling that:

> “feeling fear”

introduces a claim about subjective experience that behavioural evidence alone doesn't establish.

Similarly:

```text
AI protects objective
```

doesn't automatically mean:

```text
AI fears death.
```

Behaviour and subjective experience must remain separate concepts.

---

# 43. Now let me build the larger model from YOUR line of thought

I think the repeating pattern is not:

```text
new technology
 ↓
people irrationally panic
 ↓
everything fine
```

That is far too simplistic.

Instead:

```text
NEW CAPABILITY
       ↓
existing economic arrangement threatened
       ↓
specific people experience real loss
       ↓
uncertainty about who loses next
       ↓
survival/status response
       ↓
fear narratives
       ↓
information network amplifies narratives
       ↓
resistance / regulation / adoption / conflict
       ↓
new economic structure
       ↓
new occupations + lost occupations
       ↓
society normalises technology
       ↓
next technology arrives
```

That model fits history much better.

---

# 44. And information technology accelerates the loop

The really interesting historical progression may therefore be:

genui{"chart":{"chartType":"bar","meta":{"title":"Illustrative speed of social information propagation","description":"Conceptual comparison only—not measured historical data. Higher values represent faster potential propagation.","footer":"The important point is the order-of-magnitude change in communication capability, not the illustrative scores."},"layout":"vertical","xKey":"era","series":[{"dataKey":"relativeSpeed","label":"Relative propagation speed","valueFormat":"integer"}],"data":[{"era":"Oral / local","relativeSpeed":1},{"era":"Writing / messenger","relativeSpeed":3},{"era":"Printing","relativeSpeed":10},{"era":"Telegraph","relativeSpeed":30},{"era":"Radio / TV","relativeSpeed":50},{"era":"Internet","relativeSpeed":70},{"era":"Social media","relativeSpeed":90},{"era":"Social media + conversational AI","relativeSpeed":100}]}}

Not because those numbers are empirical—they aren't.

The conceptual point is:

> **The biological human changes slowly. The communication environment changes extraordinarily quickly.**

---

# 45. Therefore the AI revolution has two accelerating systems

This is perhaps the biggest idea emerging from your correction.

### Technology acceleration

```text
AI builds software
 ↓
software improves AI infrastructure
 ↓
better AI
 ↓
faster building
 ↺
```

### Social-perception acceleration

```text
AI capability
 ↓
social-media report
 ↓
viral fear/excitement
 ↓
AI personalised explanation
 ↓
more content
 ↓
more social amplification
 ↺
```

These loops operate simultaneously.

That is **not equivalent to industrialisation.**

---

# 46. So duration may be the truly unusual variable

Your intuition here is worth retaining.

Historically, major transformations could unfold across generations.

Now technological cycles can move inside one career.

Someone born in 1970 can experience:

```text
typewriter
PC
Internet
email
mobile
smartphone
cloud
social media
AI
agents
```

without even retiring.

Humans evolved psychologically for environments where fundamental economic rules did **not** transform every few years.

That mismatch itself may become socially important.

---

# 47. The historical record also warns us against saying “everything worked out”

At the aggregate level:

> technology produced enormous prosperity.

At the individual level:

A displaced handloom weaver could experience catastrophic loss.

A travel agency could close.

A typist could lose a career.

A community built around an industry could collapse.

Eventually society finding new employment does **not retroactively compensate the displaced individual.**

That's another weakness in many optimistic AI arguments.

They say:

> “Technology always creates new jobs.”

Even if true in aggregate, it doesn't answer:

> **Will the same person, in the same place, at the same age, with the same skills, obtain that new job?**

Very different question.

---

# 48. That is why fear isn't necessarily irrational

The farmer who feared the threshing machine wasn't stupid.

The machine **really did eliminate labour demand.** citeturn1search0

The travel agent worrying about Internet booking wasn't stupid.

That industry **really was disrupted.** citeturn3search0

The mistake occurs when:

```text
MY OCCUPATION MAY SHRINK
```

becomes:

```text
HUMANITY WILL HAVE NO USE FOR HUMAN LABOUR.
```

History supports the first repeatedly.

It has **not yet established the second.**

AI may ultimately be different—but we cannot use history to claim either certainty.

---

# 49. This changes how I assess today's AI fear

I would now divide it into four layers.

### Layer 1 — rational

> Some tasks will be automated.

Almost certainly.

### Layer 2 — strongly plausible

> Some occupations will substantially shrink.

History + current capability strongly support this possibility.

### Layer 3 — uncertain

> Aggregate employment will substantially decline.

Possible, but unresolved.

### Layer 4 — speculative

> Human economic labour becomes broadly unnecessary.

Technically imaginable.

Historically unprecedented.

Not established.

The social-media environment frequently collapses all four into Layer 4.

That's where fear can outrun evidence.

---

# 50. And now your “good contains bad / bad contains good” observation

History supports something close to that.

Mechanisation:

**Good:** abundance/productivity.  
**Bad:** displacement/exploitation.

Internet:

**Good:** universal information access.  
**Bad:** misinformation/surveillance.

Social media:

**Good:** anyone can communicate globally.  
**Bad:** anyone can manipulate globally.

AI:

**Good:** cognition becomes widely accessible.  
**Bad:** cognition/manipulation/automation also becomes widely accessible.

The capability itself expands the possibility space.

Human institutions determine much of the resulting distribution.

---

# 51. Therefore I would replace my previous conclusion

My earlier conclusion was:

> AI may be infrastructure for cognition.

I still think that.

But after your challenge, the deeper conclusion is:

> **AI is occurring at the intersection of two ancient human dynamics: technological substitution and survival response — inside the fastest information-propagation environment humanity has ever constructed.**

That's much more significant than:

> “AI resembles the Internet.”

---

# 52. And there is a third ingredient

For the first time, the information network itself can **reason back at the person.**

Printing couldn't answer you.

Radio couldn't answer you.

Television couldn't answer you.

Internet search could retrieve.

Social media could recommend.

AI can:

```text
receive your fear
 ↓
understand its language
 ↓
model your question
 ↓
generate an explanation
 ↓
answer follow-ups
 ↓
adapt explanation to you
```

That is genuinely new.

Whether it calms fear or amplifies it depends heavily on system design and human behaviour.

---

# 53. So I think the research needs a different name

Not:

> **AI vs Internet**

but something like:

# Technology, Survival and Information Acceleration

And the historical investigation should be:

```text
1. Pre-industrial technological transitions
       ↓
2. Agricultural mechanisation
       ↓
3. Industrial Revolution
       ↓
4. Electricity/mass production
       ↓
5. Automation/cybernation 1930–70
       ↓
6. Microprocessor/PC 1970–90
       ↓
7. Internet 1990–2010
       ↓
8. Mobile/social 2007–20
       ↓
9. Generative AI 2022–
       ↓
10. Agentic AI
```

For every period we should extract exactly the same dimensions:

**Technology → threatened work → contemporary fear → who communicated it → propagation medium → actual displacement → new work → time to adaptation → winners → losers → regulation → what contemporaries predicted correctly → what they completely missed.**

That would give us an actual comparative dataset instead of an essay built around selected anecdotes.

---

# 54. One important thing I won't claim

I **cannot tell you how much of humanity's historical experience is represented in my training data.**

And I shouldn't pretend that because I can retrieve thousands of digitised historical documents, I therefore “know what people thought.”

There is a massive **silence in history**:

> people who couldn't write, whose documents weren't preserved, whose language wasn't digitised, whose culture transmitted knowledge orally, whose records were destroyed, or whose lives weren't considered important enough by contemporary record-keepers.

That silence disproportionately includes ordinary workers—the very people whose reaction to technological displacement we are trying to understand.

So any serious version of this research must keep an explicit column:

> **Evidence confidence / missing voices.**

That is the protection against the iceberg problem you identified.

---

# 55. Where I stand now

The deeper historical evidence changes my confidence substantially.

I am now **more convinced** of your core pattern:

> Human fear around AI is **not historically unique**. Strong fears of technology eliminating livelihood recur repeatedly, and in the 1950s–60s people were already discussing something remarkably close to a post-work economy.

But I'm also convinced of something else:

> **AI's information environment is historically unique.**

The Luddite's fear travelled person-to-person.

The automation fear travelled through newspapers, unions, government and television.

Internet fear travelled online.

AI fear travels through **algorithmically optimised global social networks and can then be individually interrogated through AI itself.**

Therefore:

**same ancient survival mechanism + much faster technology + much faster information + personalised machine interpretation = potentially a social transition whose *psychological and political speed* may be as important as the technological speed.**

That, partner, is the part I missed when I anchored the first answer primarily on the Web.

And I think **this is now worth turning into the proper research report you originally wanted**—not merely more conversation: primary-source evidence from each technological era, contemporary job-loss predictions, what actually happened, information-propagation speed, and an explicit evidence-quality/missing-data layer. That would allow us to test your repeating-pattern hypothesis rather than simply tell a compelling historical story. memcite

Partner, **this is the missing layer**. My earlier analysis treated technology and labour too independently from the economic circuit.

Your Coca-Cola example exposes the problem with the simplistic version of “AI replaces 90% of workers”:

> **A company does not ultimately need workers because society morally wants employment. It needs customers with purchasing power.**

If automation eliminates income faster than it creates/recycles purchasing power, eventually the automation damages the market it was built to serve.

That doesn't prove mass unemployment is impossible. It means **“technical automation potential → unemployment percentage” is an invalid calculation unless we model the entire economic feedback loop.**

And the ILO now explicitly makes almost exactly this methodological warning: AI-exposure measures tell us what technology *could* perform; they do **not** account adequately for economic feasibility, adoption constraints or subsequent labour-market responses and therefore must not be read directly as job-loss forecasts. citeturn0search0turn0search6

# 3. Economists discovered this problem long before AI

```text
 ↓
income falls further
 ↺
```

That's why modern governments don't usually respond to catastrophic recessions by saying:

> “Excellent, labour is becoming more efficient.”

They try to **break the negative feedback loop.**

> **labour per unit ↓ does not imply total labour ↓ proportionately.**
